utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can the interpreters hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Marc Dubuisson, can you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Niemann, can we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Niemann, and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I am Goran Mikulicic representing the Defence, together with my colleague, Mr. Joka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning to Mr. Aleksovski too. Can you hear me well? Are you feeling well today? Did you take some fresh air?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honours -- thank you for your interest, Your Honours. In the morning, one feels fresh, but we will see as the day progresses. I must say yesterday was a very difficult day for me, and I found it hard towards the end, but we'll see how things will work out today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. You may be seated. Mr. Meddegoda, it is up to you now. According to what you said, you need one hour forty-five minutes, but as we already said yesterday, we can make a gift to you of some additional time, if necessary. But you may continue, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I thank you. Your Honours, if I may start from where I left yesterday recounting the evidence? Witness I, Your Honours, is another detainee who had been wounded by fragmentation bullets whilst digging trenches on the front lines. The next day, despite his wounded hand, an HVO soldier had entered his cell and hit him really hard, as the witness said, "so that I had a bruise, a black eye, for almost two months." The witness had then been questioned by the accused and asked "whether I had hit myself while digging with a shovel or with a pickaxe." Though the witness had informed the accused he had been hit by an HVO soldier "who simply entered the cell," no action had been taken against him. Witness H, Your Honours, remembered that together with HVO soldiers, there were also soldiers wearing HV insignia, soldiers belonging to the Croatian army at the time he was arrested on 15 April, 1993. The witness, Your Honours, testified that the accused described Kaonik as "a military prison and a concentration camp ..." and he was "commander of all the military that were with him in the barracks compound." He also described the shooting that took place on one occasion which resulted in injuries being caused to two detainees when HVO soldiers had prevented them from running for cover. On the same day, Your Honours, in Rovna, where they had been digging trenches, the witness had observed both soldiers of the HVO and the Croatian army. He had, in fact, been hit by a soldier of the Croatian army wearing HVO insignia when he asked for some water to drink. In private session, Your Honours, the witness described the incident involving his brother who escaped from Kaonik camp. After the escape, the witness had been questioned by the accused, after which they had been separated into solitary confinement, and Dzemo, Mario Maric, and Goran Medjugorac had entered his cell and he had been savagely beaten. He said "the first time only Dzemo hit me in the face, then he hit me again with his fist, about three or four times ... he hit me on the stomach ... and I fell to the ground." "I'm not sure whether all of them were beating me, but I could feel the blows coming one after another ... from that I concluded that all three were beating me." "... they went to the other three men who were also placed in solitary cells, and of course they were beaten too and I know this because I could hear their screams ... they returned to my cell again and applied the same system ... they beat me again." At one point in time, the accused had come escorted by the three men, and when "I could not reply and did not know what to say, he left and the three of them continued to beat me." The witness testified, Your Honours, that he still suffers consequences from those beatings. He also said, Your Honours, that during the period of his detention, he heard beatings and screams very often and "especially the man from Syria ... was beaten frequently." Referring to the accused's authority, the witness said that Zlatko Aleksovski introduced himself as "... the warden of the entire prison" and from what was apparent to him, "was in control of the military there." Your Honours, another witness, Edib Zlotrg, recalled the words of an elderly man who had said to him that "killings were quite usual and people ... often got wounded while trench digging." On 25th April, he and a group of prisoners had been to Kratine where they dug trenches until the following morning. At Kratine, the group of detainees had been subjected to verbal abuse and maltreatment, where Miroslav Bralo, alias Cicko, an HVO member, claimed that he had killed about 80 women and children. Bralo had taught them "to make the sign of the cross" and, in fact, had threatened to kill one man who had not been able to make the sign properly. On another occasion, Bralo had got three young men to clean the field with their teeth, with their hands tied behind their backs. Thereafter "he took them to a pond in the vicinity ... and we never saw these three young men again. They were probably slaughtered," lamented the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, please take your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honours, Witness E's testimony corroborates the evidence of other witnesses regarding the beating and torture perpetrated on the eleven Arabs and a man from Travnik in solitary confinement. From the cells in which these detainees were held, "often cries were heard ... They were maltreated and beaten." Going into private session, Your Honours, the witness corroborated the evidence of Witness H regarding the escape of a detainee and the beating and torture that followed. He said, Aleksovski arrived with Dzemo and another soldier and they hit him several times, after which the accused, Dzemo, and the other soldier came to his cell, questioned him, and "hit me several times." The questioning had been done by Aleksovski, and Dzemo and the soldier had hit him with a club and fists while the accused "was just watching, stood there watching," as the witness said. After that the accused had said, "Let us carry on with the interrogation." According to this witness, they had again been subject to beating and torture, being beaten by "Dzemo with his club and this other guy started to beat me again ... I fell into a corner, they continued beating me" until "my nose was broken ... I had bruises, I was black and blue ... I was all bloody, my face was in blood" whilst Zlatko Aleksovski "was standing by the door" giving "signs with his eyes and his head and sort of gave them the go-ahead" for the beatings. Despite these injuries, he had not been taken for medical treatment, and in cross-examination, when questioned as to why he did not complain about this inhuman treatment to the ICRC or the ECMM, the witness replied that "whenever we complained we would end up receiving double" and illustrated his answer with an incident involving "two people from Loncari, two young men who had come back from trench-digging and were wounded, one in the head and the other in the neck, were taken to see a doctor, they never came back and to the present day nobody knows what happened to them ..." Witness J, Your Honours, arrested and detained in Kaonik in April of 1993, testified about the incident involving 30 detainees, including his son, who had been taken to Rovna in the presence of the accused. Unfortunately, Your Honours, his son, who at the time was in the prime of his youth, aged 21, never returned. Later he learnt from another detainee who had been digging trenches with his son that he had been "wounded by a bullet that grazed the back of his head." Some days later, he had been taken to the accused's office where Zarko Petrovic had acknowledged that his son had been wounded. Petrovic had also said, "I just can see to it that you are not sent for trench-digging anymore." Despite this undertaking, Your Honours, the next morning the witness had been taken to Podjele to dig trenches, on which occasion he was subjected to verbal abuse. The witness also referred to another incident on 17 April, 1993, when he saw three Muslim detainees, Saban, Abdulah, and Camil Osmancevic, who had been brought to Kaonik camp the previous night, being called out by the accused, referring to them as "three birds who arrived yesterday." The accused had come to the hangar in the company of the three police officers who had tied their hands and taken them away in a car, and "we have not heard anything about them ever since," the witness said. Testifying before Your Honours, Witness U summarised the conditions in the hangar in one word, as being terrible. Even this word, despite his advanced years, was taken to dig trenches on numerous occasions in hazardous conditions. He had also witnessed a man in the hangar being beaten by some HVO men, as he put it. On another occasion, a young man who had gone with him to fetch water had been beaten. He had also seen the incident narrated by Witness J when the three young birds were taken away. Fuad Kaknjo, Your Honour, was the president of the executive council of the Vitez municipal assembly, in which capacity he was the head of the local government of Vitez. Testifying at length, Your Honours, about the multiparty elections of 1990, he explained the political processes and the socio-political identities of the parties that participated in the elections. The witness referred to the rising tension and the conflicts between the Croats and the Muslims and the various incidents that took place in the area after the takeover of the Vitez municipality building and the police station in June 1992 and the attempts made to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting, but I think we have to go a little more slowly, because I see in the transcript Fuad Kaknjo, and we know that he was a mechanical engineer, but the French interpretation told me that he was a mechanic. I think a mechanical engineer is different from just a mechanic. So as to avoid subsequent corrections, perhaps we need to go more slowly. As I told you, Mr. Meddegoda, if you don't breathe well, you will not manage to reach the end. If you need more time, we will give it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Meddegoda.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The witness, Your Honours, then referred to the rising tension and the conflicts between the Croats and the Muslims and the various incidents that took place in the area after the takeover of the Vitez municipality building and the police station in June 1992 and the attempts made to calm down the situation. In November 1992, an attempt had been made by the HVO to force the witness to surrender authority of the executive council. These and other incidents, Your Honours, had preceded the HVO attack on 16 April, 1993 leading to his arrest. During the period of the detention in Kaonik, the witness had been subjected to interrogations and beatings. He had been interrogated by the HVO within and outside the camp and had been subjected to psychological torture. He had been interrogated in the intervention squad building within the Kaonik camp by Zarko Petrovic. As a result of the beatings he received, the witness had suffered bruises around his eyes and his kidney. After this interrogation, the witness had been taken back to a cell from where he had overheard a telephone conversation where Svabo had said: "Commander, everything is fine here. I have finished my job." Your Honours, Witness Sivro, a senior official in the local administration of Vitez prior to and during the conflict, said that with the establishment of the HZHB, there developed "a tendency on the part of the Croatian authorities to dominate over the Muslim population." According to the evidence of Mr. Sivro, the Croats began to take over buildings housing government institutions, including "the police station, the post office, the municipality building, and more or less all public institutions that existed at the time, and this happened by force." "The Croatian flag with the checkerboard insignia was also hoisted at public enterprises to indicate their control," he said. He testified about a military parade organised by the HVO in late 1992, during which the soldiers had to take an oath of allegiance to the homeland. The parade commanded by Mario Cerkez had been attended by Dario Kordic, Tihomir Blaskic, and other prominent political and military leaders of the HVO. Testifying about an incident which took place on 20 October, 1992 which resulted in the killing of a member of the Muslim army, the witness said that this was the beginning of the deterioration of relations between the Croats and the Muslims. "Business premises, shops and cafes, anything that was Muslim property was destroyed either by explosives or physical force." He too had been subjected to interrogation by the HVO on more than one occasion, and corroborating the testimony of Fuad Kaknjo, he testified as having seen visible bruises and traces of beatings on the shoulders and cheeks of Kaknjo. Your Honours, I submit that his testimony is consistent with the evidence of other Prosecution witnesses on all material particulars. Dzido Osmancevic, Your Honours, said that together with him HVO soldiers arrested a group of persons from his village and took them to Kaonik camp where they were subjected to the routine of search, registration, and incarceration. He said that at times when they returned from trench digging, the accused was present at the second hangar, at the entrance to the second hangar. He would have in his hand the list with our names, and he would ask, "Are they all there?" In private session, the witness described the events following the escape of a detainee which is consistent with and corroborative of the testimony of other witnesses on this point. Hamdo Dautovic, Your Honours, described at length his arrest and the brutality that accompanied his transportation to Kaonik. He had been subjected to severe beatings and cruel interrogation. On one occasion, "I was standing for as long as I could stand while they beat me. Then I sat down when they beat me. At the end, Brane sat on my back and beat me. I was lying on my stomach. There was a microphone of some sort ... in front of my mouth. Then they went on beating me, and I was told to repeat whatever they said. So that's what I did. I repeated what they told me. This was accompanied by blows ..." On another occasion, he had been taken out of the cell and badly beaten up. Your Honours, we also remember that the witness recalled an incident where he, together with three others, were forced to enact a "monodrama," as he called it, where "we had to lie down on our backs and create a cross" and sing as ordered by the guards. "There was a lot of humiliation on that occasion, and Zlatko was amongst them. They talked, chatted and beat us. We were at their mercy, lying down, and this went on," he said. There were no facilities for religious observances except "in my thoughts and in my wishes, but that too without success," the witness said. Upon complaining to the accused about his physical condition, the witness had been taken to the Busovaca health centre, and upon inquiry by the doctor, the accused had said that the witness was suffering from a cold and needed an injection and that nothing else was wrong with him. However, the witness had told the doctor that he had blood in his stools and urine, and the witness went on. Seeing that "I was completely black and blue," the doctor told the warden, "this is animal behaviour," and said that the witness needed treatment, and, in fact, she had said so to the accused. The accused had responded that the witness had been treated and that they had a separate room in the prison for treating the sick, and therefore he did not stay in hospital. When returning to the camp, the witness had pleaded with the accused to "cut down on my portions of food because I cannot eat because of all the beatings," and the accused had assured that "nobody will beat you anymore." However, Your Honours, according to the witness, from then on, "I was beaten more. I received more beatings ... I regretted having complained to the warden because I was receiving more beatings," the witness said. The witness identified a guard in the camp by the name of Medjugorac as the person "who beat me the most and who told me that I would not come out alive from them. He beat me the most, and for me, it was like a death sentence when he would be there because there would always be beatings ... and if anybody wanted to beat any of the prisoners, I was the one." Describing the attitude of the guards, he said, "They would say we had some drinks but we did not have any snacks, so we need some snacks. What do we do?" Then I would be beaten, that would be the snack. "The worst moment would be as the cell was being unlocked and the expectation of being beaten. Then it was the beatings themselves. Ten/twenty blows, kicks, I became immune to the beatings in the end," he said. In answer to a question as to whether he was aware if any of the guards who beat him were punished by the camp commander, the witness said, "I think they were rewarded by the warden ..." On the day of his release, Hamdo had overheard Goran Medjugorac say to the warden, "Did you not promise me that Dautovic would not leave alive," in response to which the accused had said, "You see, he's going to die anyway, so it is better that he dies in their custody than ours." The witness compared his release from prison "as if I had been born again, going from death to life." Witness T, Your Honours, was another witness who had suffered severe beating and torture whilst in detention. On the way to Kaonik, he had been beaten with rifle butts, and in Kaonik, they had started torturing him. He had been kicked in the head and around the kidneys with military boots. They also jumped on him. This torture and beating had lasted for about 10 minutes. In the evening, the accused had come into his cell accompanied by Dzemo and Medjugorac. He said that, early on in the day, the accused had cursed him, "swearing at Islam." Inside his cell, the accused had kicked him on the chest, and then on the accused's instructions, Medjugorac had started kicking him and jumping on his body. All along during this beating and torture, the accused had been present. The consequences of this was that "my body was all blackened, marked, and my eyes were black because of the torture." His body had been "bloated as a result of the kicking and the beating ..." and he had been "bleeding through his nose and mouth." He had also noticed blood in his urine. Referring to the long-term consequences of the beatings and torture, the witness said: "... to date I suffer from continuous migraine, I cannot concentrate, and when I am asleep, I cannot breathe properly, kidney pains ... I started suffering from chest pains and heart disorders, and I have reached the point where I have given up trying to find out exactly what is wrong with me." Your Honours, I would now like to deal with the rebuttal evidence led by the Prosecution. It was the Defence case that the detainees who were taken to the Busovaca health centre and ordered treatment and therapy at home were, in fact, sent home. Your Honours, in order to rebut this assertion of the Defence, the Prosecution summoned Witnesses V and W to testify. It was the testimony of Witness V that, whilst in detention, his condition deteriorated, and upon being taken to the health centre, "treatment at home" had been recommended. Ignoring this recommendation, the camp commander had made a gesture "meaning nothing doing." Not only did the accused ignore the doctor's recommendation, the very next day, he also permitted the witness to be taken for hard labour, to dig graves and bury some dead. The following morning, together with other detainees, he was taken to Kula to dig trenches on the front lines of the HVO. Witness W was also in similar circumstances. During the period of his detention, his condition had deteriorated, and he had been taken to the health centre where, after examination, he had been told "to go home and get therapy." Again, ignoring this recommendation, the camp commander had ordered that the witness be detained in a cell. Not only did the accused ignore the doctor's recommendation, the very next day, he too was sent to Kula to dig trenches on the front lines of the HVO in hazardous conditions. Your Honours, amongst the witnesses from the International Community, Charles McLeod, who served with the European Commission Monitoring Mission in the former Yugoslavia, testified inter alia about his visit to Kaonik prison on 10 May, 1995 accompanying Jean Pierre Thebault. The entrance to the camp had been manned by guards in military uniform. At the meeting with the accused, the witness took down notes during most of the conversation. It is the evidence of Mr. McLeod that, during the course of the meeting, the accused had said that he lives in the Kaonik camp and acknowledged his professional skills as a prison officer, having worked in the Zenica prison. Being a professional prison officer, he had understood how a prison should be administered, and "therefore," if I may quote the witness's words, "he was saying he had an understanding of how the Geneva Conventions should be applied to the running of a prison, and he was also using his knowledge as a professional gaoler to ensure that the prison was run along the lines in which he ran it." The accused had also acknowledged the poor conditions in Kaonik camp. At the time of the visit, there had been 79 Muslim prisoners, whilst the numbers had been more in April and early May, with 107 prisoners on 16 April and 109 on 9 May, 1993. He had acknowledged that both soldiers and civilians were detained in the camp, and at most times, it is the poor who have neither the affluence nor the influence that are detained, and that none of the Muslims have been charged for violating the law and that, for the most part, the detainees were teachers and engineers. The accused had admitted his knowledge of the Geneva Conventions and admitted that "more or less all the rules of the Geneva Conventions are obeyed in most cases." Admitting his knowledge of detainees being taken out to dig trenches, the accused had acknowledged that the provisions of the Geneva Conventions "do not allow prisoners to be taken out for any work if their lives are in danger," having "been warned about that by the ICRC as well." As testified by Mr. McLeod, the accused had, in fact, admitted his responsibility with regard to the prisoners detained in Kaonik camp. He had also admitted his knowledge of mistreatment of the prisoners by the guards. During the course of the meeting, the accused had, in fact, taken the decision to release a detainee, when the witness queried as to the basis of his detention. The witness said, if I may quote, he "... commented quietly that if it had been me, I would have sent him to Zenica rather than putting him into a cell. Aleksovski said that in that case, since the man was clearly a civilian, we could take him back to Zenica with us. He told the man to take his coat and leave the cell. While we were still talking, they organised a car to take him back to the point where he had been picked up." Your Honours, this is a clear demonstration that the accused not only acknowledges everything that went on in the camp but also exercised command and control over everything that took place within it, including the detainees, the guards, and the soldiers. The Prosecution, Your Honours, also tendered through this witness Exhibit P7, a computer printout of a list of Muslim prisoners being held as at that date given to him by the accused. Describing what he said whilst visiting some cells, the witness said there were detainees "dressed in civilian clothing and appeared to be civilians. There were certainly two soldiers that we met, but they were introduced as Croatian military prisoners who had committed some unspecified crime. They were dressed in uniform," he said. According to Mr. McLeod, despite their request to "talk to the prisoners privately," guards were always present in the cells, and he was quite sure that "had the opportunity been there, then people would have liked to have told us precisely what was going on." He reiterated his position that the prisoners were "men between 20 and 40 and 50," whilst some were "certainly quite old," "wearing basically civilian clothes of various sorts" except the "couple of Croatian military prisoners who were in uniform." Confirming that there were differences in the treatment afforded to Croatian prisoners as opposed to Muslim prisoners, the witness said there had been a clear difference in the number of people detained in each cell with "more than four and probably less than ten to a cell, whereas there were only two Croatian military prisoners both sharing a cell," and the cells "certainly did not appear to have been designed for the number of people we saw in most of them ..." The Croatian soldiers in the prison "looked fit and healthy and cheerful" with a room "full of what appeared to be their personal possessions" whilst the other detainees "certainly did not appear to have any personal possessions or significant personal possessions with them, so one could see a difference there ..." Your Honours, Mr. Junhov, also a member of the European Community Monitoring Mission, testified that upon receiving information about the existence of Kaonik camp, he, together with a German colleague and an interpreter, had visited Kaonik on 1st April, 1993. Upon arrival, he had met with a person who "introduced himself as being in charge of the prison," with whom they had visited the prison taking photographs. One of the buildings, he said, by its size and design, appeared to be like a "Swedish army's ordinary munition stores." Entering the building with the cells, the commander described it "as a prison" where "ordinary criminals" are detained. Upon further inquiry, he had found a man in solitary confinement serving a 10-year prison sentence and, in another cell, five persons who had been arrested, according to the commander, because "they are foreigners" without passports or documents. However, the five prisoners described themselves as "missionaries ... supporting the Muslim people in Bosnia from Egypt, Pakistan, Tunisia and Algeria" being detained without any rhyme or reason. Upon inquiry, one of them had responded "I do not know, I have done nothing criminal, I was just arrested and put in here." None of them had been "accused of any crimes." Describing the conditions in this particular camp, he said it was "not acceptable to keep people in such conditions" and there were "very bad standards in all aspects in the prison." The conditions in the cells appeared to be "very dirty" with "a smell that was awful" and the prisoners were "very dirty, unshaven, wearing dirty clothes" without the opportunity for "a shower for the last one month." Being upset by these conditions, he had discussed this with the commander who acknowledged his familiarity with the Geneva Conventions, a copy of which he said "was on his desk." Expressing his opinion to the commander, Mr. Junhov had said that "the conditions in the prison were not in accordance with the Convention."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Meddegoda, excuse me for interrupting you. I wanted to ask you how much more time you need.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I should be -- I was hoping to finish by the first break, which should be taken by about 10.45, so I should be able to finish around 10.45 or shortly thereafter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may continue then. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Testifying further, Your Honours, Mr. Junhov said that Muslim people were detained for "no reason at all, just as some kind of bargain chips or something to have to exchange for something else." During his mission, he claimed to have seen HOS soldiers in black uniform belonging to Croatian military units other than the HVO in "different locations throughout Central Bosnia" and whenever they saw these HOS units "You can bet there will be trouble," he said. This was something that always proved to be true. In cross-examination, referring to the commander's control of the camp, the witness said it was his "impression ... when you ... talk to him, and his way of behaviour and so on ... there was no doubt that he was in charge - he was responsible for at least that building, and I had the opinion that he was responsible for the whole area." It was also his consistent position that the attire worn by the commander and guards was similar to what was being worn by Croatian soldiers all over Bosnia-Herzegovina. Without dwelling at length, Your Honours, on Witness K's testimony, Your Honours will recall that he tendered into evidence two maps depicting the front lines held by the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was his testimony that the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina had trenches right along the front lines. The soldiers of the BH army had dug their own trenches and nobody other than soldiers had been used for this purpose. However, as far as the digging of trenches by the HVO was concerned, he had heard through reports from the commanders on the ground that in addition to soldiers, civilians held captive under HVO control were also employed to dig trenches. He had also heard, again from reports, that civilians were being used as human shields by the HVO. Daniel Damon, a freelance journalist for Sky News, testifying before Your Honours' Tribunal, said that whilst visiting Tomislavgrad in Bosnia during the period of autumn 1992, he had sent "plenty of Croatian troops ... troops of the Croatian forces, and it was a base for the Croatian forces going in and out of Bosnia ... and it was also an important police point for the Croatian authorities on the border and inside Bosnia." He said that it was the assumption of "most if not all journalists that the forces inside Bosnia wearing the Croatian insignia were from both sides of the Bosnian-Croatian border ... It seemed to be obvious from both the political background and the logistical background that these troops were - some of them local Bosnian Croats and some of them Croats from inside Croatia." Citing a clear example, he claimed having seen " ... a vehicle with HV plates and troops ... as opposed to an HVO plate, just inside the border on its way to Tomislavgrad." He said that they had not taken much notice of the distinction of HV and HVO troops because for them " ... troops wearing HV and HVO insignia ... were the same." He too described the conditions in Kaonik as "inhuman," with the prisoners have no access to water and looking very dirty and "from what I was told by the prisoners, they were not being treated well," the witness testified. Your Honours, I will now deal with the testimony of Professor Bianchini. Prosecution Exhibit P36, Your Honours, was very exhaustive of the witness's credentials and expertise and speaks for itself. His evidence Your Honours, went virtually unchallenged, and for that reason I would urge Your Honours to act on that evidence. Commencing his testimony with the political composition of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, he went on to deal with, inter alia, the impact of the 1st and 2nd World Wars on the former Yugoslavia, Tito's ascendancy to power and the different constitutional models of Tito's Yugoslavia, the factors that led to the break-up of the former Yugoslavia, the ascendancy of the present political leadership in the different republics, the plebiscites in the different republics, and the declarations of independence, the structure of the armed forces prior to and post 1991, the ethnic composition, and the emergence of political parties. He then went on to deal with the political and military structures of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia and the relationship between the Republic of Croatia and the HDZ in Croatia on the one hand and Croatia and the Bosnian Croats, the HZ-HB and the HVO, on the other. It was Professor Bianchini's evidence that Croatia gave political, military, and economic support to the Bosnian Croats, supplying them with finances, weapons, ammunition, and personnel, and he tendered documentary evidence in support thereof. The Prosecution would also strongly urge Your Honours to consider the evidence of Witness X whose testimony in the Blaskic trial has been admitted into evidence in this trial. It was only very recently that the Prosecution apprised the Trial Chamber of the value of this evidence and its relevancy in establishing conclusively, inter alia, Croatia's policy towards Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia's involvement in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in rebutting the testimony of Admiral Domazet. Therefore, Your Honours, Witness X's evidence regarding Croatian assistance to and control of the HVO during the war provides support to the Prosecution's contention that there was an international armed conflict in the Busovaca area during the period relevant to this indictment and that the crimes committed in Kaonik camp were linked to this armed conflict. The record before this Trial Chamber is replete with evidence that the government of Croatia assisted, supplied, and often controlled the operations of the HVO in its operations against the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In May 1992, the Croatian army assigned HVO Brigadier Zarko Tole the task of organising the defence of Central Bosnia, which included the towns of Busovaca and Vitez. During the same month, the Croatian army began organising the training of HVO units in Herceg-Bosna. By July 1992, Croatian army units were stationed inside Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to protect the "territorial integrity and security of the Republic of Croatia." Admiral Domazet, testifying in the Blaskic trial, acknowledged that HV units were present in Bosnia and Herzegovina beginning in 1992. Indeed, Croatian army officers often commanded Bosnian Croat units and Croatian army units often directly participated in actions against Bosnian government forces within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In May 1993, for example, two brigades of the Croatian army were based in Mostar. Professor Bianchini testified that from 1992 through 1995, the HVO and the army of Croatia were essentially the same army. Thus, for purposes of the application of the grave breaches provisions of Geneva Conventions III and IV, the significant and continuous military support, military action by the armed forces of Croatia in support of the Bosnian Croats against the forces of the Bosnian government on the territory of the latter was sufficient to convert a domestic conflict between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian government into an international one. In the present case, the Prosecution has established the accused's direct participation in assaults, abusive interrogations, the denial of adequate medical care, hygiene, and nutrition, the use of civilian detainees and prisoners of wars as human shields and in forced trench-digging work on the front lines and the subjection of the Muslim detainees to beatings and other forms of physical and mental cruelty. In fact, the accused personally beat prisoners on more than one occasion. The accused also ordered the guards to beat the prisoners. By ordering the commission of the crimes referred to in the Statute of this Tribunal, the accused incurred individual criminal liability under Article 7(1). Witnesses described beatings and interrogations directed by the accused following the escape of a prisoner. The accused also led HVO soldiers in assaults on detainees within the prison. Indeed, when the accused did not actively take part in beatings, he often encouraged such behaviour by standing by and laughing and joking while prison guards and soldiers assaulted the detainees. The camp personnel used the words "dance party" to describe the acts of mistreatment, beatings, and various kinds of provocations. The accused was also directly involved in sending prisoners to dig trenches near the front lines. By all of this abhorrent conduct, the accused directly contributed to the commission of offences against the prisoners at Kaonik, thereby incurring criminal responsibility under Article 7(1). Your Honours, dealing with superior responsibility, the evidence presented at trial proved that the accused held a superior position during the time he oversaw Kaonik prison. The accused admitted that Kaonik was the military prison for all of Central Bosnia. Most of the personnel working at Kaonik were dressed as ordinary soldiers and some of them wore the HVO insignia. The entrance to the prison complex was guarded by soldiers and military policemen. The accused's former civilian colleagues in the Ministry of Justice considered Kaonik to be under military authority. "... it was a new prison, a small facility adapted from military barracks, which is what it was before." The accused told his former supervisor that he was leaving to be the warden of the military prison in Kaonik. Moreover, Your Honours, according to Blazenka Vujica, who served as the accused's secretary at the prison, Kaonik was a military prison. Ms. Vujica was a member of the military police, and that institution assigned her to be the accused's secretary at Kaonik. The accused's primary role was to oversee the organisation and functioning of the military prison. She testified that some prisoners were incarcerated in Kaonik on the orders of the district military court in Travnik. Others were serving punishments upon the orders of their commanders. When the accused issued documents, he stamped them with a seal issued by the Croatian armed forces. Ms. Vujica testified that during the armed conflict, many civilian institutions ceased to function, and the army assumed the responsibility for providing food, clothing, et cetera. During the period she worked for the accused at Kaonik, Muslim civilians were detained in a building called "the district military prison." The civilians were brought to the prison by the military police and the HVO army. The accused was responsible for all prisoners incarcerated at Kaonik regardless of their classification or status. Thus the evidence presented at trial proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused was part of the HVO chain of command. He executed orders that he received from his superiors and issued orders to his HVO subordinates. Therefore, for the purposes of the accused's superior responsibility for the offences charged in the indictment under Article 7(3), he was an integral link in the military chain of command responsible for the Kaonik prison. The evidence shows that the accused enjoyed sufficient power to take reasonable measures to deter the commission of offences at the Kaonik camp and to punish the perpetrators. As commander of the Kaonik prison, the accused exercised a specific mandate which supported the Croatian war effort. According to the accused's own witnesses, he oversaw the day-to-day operation of the prison, carried out orders from above, and issued orders to his subordinates. It is my submission that the Prosecution has presented ample evidence at trial to prove that the accused was the commander of the Kaonik prison, that he exercised power and authority over the camp officials who served under him, including the power to control the actions of subordinates and to punish them for offences. Your Honours, the accused's own admissions serve as the best evidence of his position of authority. Habitually, he introduced himself to new arrivals at Kaonik as the commander of the prison. Witness O testified how, after he introduced himself, the accused cynically reassured the detainees that they had nothing to be afraid of, that they were safe. The following day, 15 men in his group were taken out to serve as human shields for the HVO forces. The accused told another group of new prisoners that "I am the director of Kaonik prison, and you are now my responsibility." Indeed, the accused had the power to release Muslim civilians from prison. The accused's secretary acknowledged that he commanded the prison: " ... we worked at the orders of Mr. Aleksovski, so there were no problems." Indeed, the prison guards clearly respected his authority. At trial, witness Meho Sivro described his first moments in the camp: " ... this soldier who was shouting at us, he said like this: 'Whoever moves, don't you dare move, because our commander is here. You have to be quiet.'" Again, the accused's secretary described his command authority over the other prison personnel. The shift commanders were not allowed to make any instructions on their own. They were to receive instructions from the warden. When unknown persons requested permission to enter the camp, the guards on duty at the front gate would have to consult the accused before permitting the visitor to enter. Whenever new detainees were brought to Kaonik, the personnel would prepare a list with the names of the new arrivals pursuant to the instructions of the accused. When a European Community Monitoring Mission visited the camp, the accused provided the ECMM representative with a full list of the detainees imprisoned there. At the bottom of the list were the words "manager of district military prison" and the accused's name. When Kaonik prisoners were needed for forced labour on the front lines, the prison guards would obtain a list of names from the accused's office, and the prisoners who were on the list would be called out for trench digging that day. Sometimes the accused would stand by and observe that the guards carried out this task properly. On other occasions, the accused would maintain the list " ... and he would simply read five, ten men, how many were needed, and thus they would go." Periodically the accused would be present when the detainees returned to Kaonik from trench-digging and he would ask the guards if the prisoners were all there. On some occasions, some of the prisoners did not come back. Indeed, the evidence presented by the Prosecution demonstrated that the accused used his command authority and power to the mistreatment of prisoners. On one occasion, the accused ordered a guard named Zarko to beat Witness L. On another, the accused ordered a guard name Medugorac to beat Witness T. On both occasions, the prison guards immediately followed the accused's orders. Another time, the accused led a group of HVO soldiers into Witness M's cell so that the soldiers could beat Witness M and his cellmate. The accused asserted his authority over the prison in many different aspects of prison life. For example, the accused could excuse prisoners from their trench-digging assignments. Moreover, when a delegation from the ECMM visited Kaonik prison on 1 April, 1993, they were received by a man who introduced himself as the person responsible for the prison. The accused acknowledged that he knew the Geneva Conventions and that he kept a copy of it on his desk. The accused also oversaw the access of detainees to the media. When a television crew came to Kaonik camp to interview prisoners, the accused and his deputy, Marko Krilic, orchestrated the production. While the filming took place, the accused stood two to three metres away laughing and joking. Rather than fulfil his duty as a commander pursuant to the Geneva Conventions, the accused often obstructed compliance with these provisions. When Witness M told the Trial Chamber how the accused delayed his exchange because the accused held some bias against persons from his village, subsequently the accused tried to obstruct the exchange of another prisoner during negotiations with representatives of the ICRC. Just before Witness M was finally released, the accused told him that if he ever returned to Kaonik, he would not leave alive. Indeed, the accused had the power to dramatically control events within the prison because he made the rules for the prison guards who served under him. The evidence presented at trial, Your Honours, therefore proves beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused was the commander of Kaonik prison and that he affirmatively exercised his power and authority over other camp personnel and the prisoners. The evidence also demonstrates that the accused ignored his command duty to adequately instruct his subordinates regarding the proper treatment of prisoners held under his authority. In this case, the evidence shows that, at all relevant times, the accused had executive authority over Kaonik prison. The abuses committed against Muslim detainees in the camp were not just widespread and notorious. The accused himself participated in many of them. Given the information available to him, the accused therefore bore a duty to take all appropriate measures to stop further mistreatment. This duty was even greater given the accused's control over the prison personnel. Indeed, the accused had the power and ability to dramatically control events within the camp because he made the rules of the prison guards who served under him. None of the shift commanders dared to issue instructions on their own. In sum, the accused "regulated life in prison." The accused, Your Honours, had the ability to officiate criminal investigations of prisoner mistreatment. He did so on at least one occasion in February 1993 when two Muslim prisoners were killed. Although the accused consulted with the judge of the district military court in Mostar about these killings, he never mentioned other abuses constantly being perpetrated by HVO soldiers against the detainees. Considering this evidence, Your Honours, it is my submission that the Prosecution has established that the accused bore a duty to the prisoners at Kaonik, that he exercised control over the prison personnel, and that he had the ability to initiate criminal proceedings regarding abuses committed against the detainees. The accused had the ability to control the prison guards, but he failed to do so. Additionally, there is overwhelming direct evidence illustrating that the accused was fully aware that prisoners of war and civilians were brutalised within the prison camp that he commanded, as well as the deplorable conditions under which the detainees lived. "If you return," the accused warned one prisoner upon his release from Kaonik, "you won't get out alive." The Prosecution has also proved beyond reasonable doubt that the accused was aware that HVO soldiers mistreated the civilian detainees. Moreover, the use of these prisoners for labour detachments took place with the knowledge and approval of the accused. On at least one occasion, an ICRC representative warned the accused that the prisoners should not be compelled to perform forced labour, and particularly not near the front lines. The accused would be responsible for any harm that befell the prisoners. Nevertheless, that night, about 20 prisoners were sent out to dig trenches. Witness S testified that one day, after several consecutive days of digging, his hands were covered with blisters. When he asked the accused to spare him from digging on that day, the accused simply looked at his hands and walked away, and the witness was taken out to dig again. He never received any medical treatment for his blisters. According to Witness R, the accused was present when prisoners were taken out for trench digging detail or used as human shields. He was aware of the fate that awaited some of these prisoners. Indeed, after two Muslim detainees were killed while digging trenches, the accused requested that local physicians determine the exact cause of death. There were occasions on which the accused would request that prison guards transport a detainee to Busovaca for medical attention. When Witness W, who suffered from thrombosis, received a prescription from a physician to obtain therapy at home instead of in the Kaonik prison and Witness W presented the prescription to the accused, the accused glanced at the paper and instructed the guards to move Witness W to another cell. Subsequently, Witness W had to join the trench digging detail. Nor can the accused claim that he was ignorant of proper prison standards. His former secretary testified that "... he knew the rules in penitentiaries ... He had one copy of the house rules from the penitentiary in Zenica and the district prison in Zenica, and I still have it," she said. Pursuant to these regulations, convicts were never asked to work in dangerous circumstances and always had access to medical care, nor could physical force be used as part of the "resocialisation process." Finally, Your Honours, Hamdo Dautovic told the Trial Chamber how he was constantly beaten during his detention at Kaonik. One of the camp guards, Medjugorac, would tell Dautovic that he would not leave the prison alive. On the day of his release to members of ICRC, Medjugorac protested to the accused, "Did you not promise me that Dautovic would not leave alive?" The accused patiently explained to his subordinate his decision to free the prisoner. "You see he is going to die anyway, so it is better that he dies in their custody than ours." Accordingly, for the purpose of liability under Article 7(3), the Prosecution has demonstrated that the accused had actual knowledge of violations of international humanitarian law that were committed against Muslim prisoners whilst he was commander of the Kaonik prison. Your Honours, the Prosecution also presented evidence concerning the accused's direct participation and encouragement of prisoner abuse at Kaonik. The accused's failure to control his actions, as well as the conduct of his subordinates, constituted an illegal disregard for their behaviour and a malicious contempt for the welfare of the detainees at Kaonik. The accused explained to Charles McLeod that Muslim civilians were interned for their own protection. Indeed, during the same conversation, the accused subsequently confessed that his acts and omissions breached his legal duty to the prisoners "... because I know that the Geneva Conventions do not allow prisoners to be taken for any work if their lives are in danger. I have been warned about that by the ICRC as well ..." The testimony of Witness M, Your Honours, describing the accused's conduct during a visit by members of the International Red Cross, illustrates the accused's contemptuous attitude for principles of international humanitarian law. "For a while, I was taking food to this cell, and I saw that the man who was kept there was in a horrible condition, that he had been beaten and mistreated, and I thought it was terrible ... He was beaten up every day, he was abused ... When the International Red Cross came to visit us, they went from cell to cell to see who was there. When they came to cell number 4, Mr. Aleksovski was with this gentleman from the Red Cross and ... when the gentleman from the Red Cross asked why this cell was locked, he said that this was some kind of storage room and that there was no need for them to enter there. There was no need for them to see it." In this case, given his power, control, and authority as commander of Kaonik prison, the accused could have issued orders prohibiting the mistreatment of the prisoners. Alternatively, he could have punished those subordinates who committed abuses. At a minimum, the accused could have reported the excesses to the district military court. Nor does the suggestion by several Defence witnesses that the wartime conditions in and around Busovaca prevented the accused from providing better conditions for the Kaonik detainees, find support in international humanitarian law. The jurisprudence from International Tribunals clearly state that it is particularly during wartime, when innocent persons are often exposed to terrible suffering, that individuals must exercise all due care to protect the most fundamental human rights. The fact that the accused in this case did not directly order all of the crimes committed against the detainees in Kaonik does not absolve him from criminal responsibility in relation to these acts. Mr. Aleksovski's knowing failure to punish those subordinates responsible for this misconduct or otherwise prevent further mistreatment of prisoners provides a basis for liability under international law. The Prosecution presented evidence to establish that, during the time that the accused was the commander of Kaonik prison, Muslim detainees were repeatedly subjected to inhumane treatment, such as murder, beatings, unsanitary conditions, forced labour, interruption of religious activities, and theft of personal property. The overwhelming evidence of repeated mistreatment and abuse would suffice to infer the intent to damage the physical, mental, and moral integrity of the prisoners at the Kaonik detention facility. Equally obvious is the severe pain, suffering, and injuries that the prisoners endured, as well as the loss of their humanity. These incidents, Your Honours, were manifestly cruel. They project a singular intent and purpose: To inflict horrible pain and suffering on the prisoners in Kaonik. There is simply no other more benign rational to explain this conduct. Furthermore, the Prosecution presented abundant evidence to prove that these incidents and many others like them caused great suffering to the victims in the prison. A number of witnesses also testified as to the serious injuries that they received as a result of mistreatment in the Kaonik prison. Finally, prisoners were also wounded by gunfire and shelling, and some perished while digging trenches around the front line. By placing the detainees in a position of such obvious mortal danger, the personnel of the prison exhibited a wanton and reckless disregard for their safety. This evidence demonstrates that the Muslim detainees at Kaonik suffered serious injury to their bodies and health during the relevant times mentioned in the indictment. Moreover, these injuries were inflected intentionally or with utter disregard for their consequences. During the course of the trial, the Prosecution presented evidence to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that hundreds of Muslim civilians were illegally imprisoned for months at the Kaonik detention facility during 1993. This immoral deprivation of liberty was per se an outrage upon the personal dignity of the detainees. Additionally, these Muslim civilians were incarcerated under filthy, violent, deplorable, and terrible conditions. As mentioned above, it is precisely when persons are imprisoned or interned that the principle of respect for human life, for the human person codified in the Geneva Conventions assumes its full significance. Therefore, Your Honours, it is my submission that imprisoning anyone, even convicted criminals, under such conditions constitutes an assault upon the personal dignity of the detainees. Moreover, Your Honours, forcing prisoners to dig trenches, to serve as human shields, and to part with their personal possessions are other forms of violations of personal dignity. Civilians cannot be subjected to humiliating punishment or work. Indeed, ironically, convicted criminals serving their term in the Zenica civilian penitentiary close to Kaonik were not obligated to perform labour for the war effort because they were protected by law. All of these outrages were perpetrated against the prisoners at Kaonik during the relevant times mentioned in the indictment. This kind of abuse violated "the inherent dignity" of the Muslim prisoners. Your Honours, the evidence presented at trial demonstrates beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused bears responsibility for the acts alleged in the indictment under both Article 7(1) and 7(3). It is my submission that there is no evidence whatsoever that the accused made any effort either to punish or prevent the crimes perpetrated against the detainees in Kaonik prison. Accordingly, it is my submission that, considering the overwhelming evidence presented by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber should find the accused guilty of grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and violations of the laws and customs of war, under both Article 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of this Tribunal. Your Honours, in the words of that great jurist Justinian: "Justice is constant and perpetual wish to render to everyone his due. Consider what you think justice requires, not only the rights of the person charged but also the forgotten victims." I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready now? It is your turn. Please begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Of course the Defence is ready because it has been preparing for this moment for more than a year, since the trial started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. There is no doubt that the main purpose of this Tribunal and the main purpose of this Trial Chamber is to establish the truth, just as it is the main purpose of all court proceedings in any court of law on our planet to establish the truth, but we come here to a key point: What is, in fact, the truth, and where should we look for it? A philosophical thesis that I hold dear says that the truth, like art, is to be found in the eye of the beholder. In other words, that art is experienced through the personality of the person observing a work of art, and the same applies to the truth. However, thinking over this point as a lawyer, this is something that we cannot accept because it would, in fact, mean that the truth is a subjective comprehension of reality on the part of the person surrounded by that reality. This would apply to events, phenomena, and the experiences of that person. However, I am quite convinced that this standard of philosophy is simply not sufficient to judge and assess events that have become the subject of these proceedings, the subject of the indictment issued by my learned friends, the Prosecutors, and finally, the crucial issue of the guilt of my client, Mr. Aleksovski, who is, in fact, on trial here. Therefore, it is the submission of the Defence, and with all due respect our proposal to this Trial Chamber, that the Trial Chamber should be guided primarily by objectively-established facts, that is, the facts that can represent the truth in everybody's eye and not just in the eye of the beholder because it is well-known that an observer or a witness is limited in his knowledge, in fact, he is even handicapped as a factor of his various characteristics and properties, such as, for instance, his age, his sex, his education, his temperament, his motivation, his ability to concentrate and the like. Therefore, it is the view of the Defence that the truth about this case must be viewed in a far more complex manner than the manner suggested to us by our learned friends from the Prosecution. In my closing argument, I shall adopt an opposite order, so to speak; that is, I will first refer to matters of fact that my learned friend, Mr. Meddegoda, argued, and then matters of law, as argued by my learned friend, Mr. Niemann, and I will make conclusions regarding the whole proceedings, that means not only the evidence presented by the Defence, at the end of all this, as the final stage of my closing argument. First of all, Your Honours, the Defence assumes, in view of the fact that the exclusive goal of the formation of this Tribunal was to try events that occurred in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, that the Judges of this Tribunal, in preparing for these honourable duties, had the opportunity to get acquainted with certain general cultural, historical, political, and other relevant events which provide a background for all the cases that are being tried in this Tribunal. I am quite confident, Your Honours, that in this highly responsible duty, you must have come to the conclusion that the territory of the former Yugoslavia, and especially the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is something that is quite unique in the world today because of its numerous specificities. The conclusion to be inferred from this is that in Bosnia, nothing is simple; that the methods of analogy and comparison, when addressing events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, simply do not apply. Such methods cannot stand any test. Let me give you an example. In the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as we are now focusing on that area, armed conflicts occurred. Virtually every municipality was a case in itself with regard to those armed conflicts. In some places, there were Muslims and Croats fighting the Serbs predominantly, or, rather, the former JNA and the paramilitary Serbian and Montenegrin units. In another municipality, there was a conflict between Muslims and Serbs on the one side and the Croats on the other. In a third, there was a conflict between Croats and Muslims on the one side and Serbs and Muslims on the other. In a third place (sic), in the Cazin Krajina, clashes occurred between the Muslims themselves. So, you see, a theory of a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina, in terms of the establishment of legal standards and any kind of analogy, simply doesn't hold water. For this reason, throughout the proceedings, the Defence has insisted, and I think that we are supported by this Trial Chamber, especially in view of some decisions taken like the one on the 25th of September last year, that the events linked to the liability of my client are being viewed exclusively and only within a limited time frame and a territorial frame provided by the Prosecution without any analogies being made, without any comparisons being made. As I have said already, that nothing in Bosnia is simple, and then there is always the other side of the coin which we think we are observing, let me also say that there is the other side of the coin when it comes to quoting Prosecution witnesses, as has just been done by my learned friend, Mr. Meddegoda. With all due respect, the method used by Mr. Meddegoda to quote statements by Prosecution witnesses reminds me of a method of a cold buffet. I am not trying to be offensive, but it is simply like the situation when you go down for breakfast from your hotel room and you come across a big cold buffet with various dishes on the table; however, your desire determines what you will take. You will take a little of this, a little of that, and you don't really try everything. So I call this a method of a cold buffet. That was the method applied with the Prosecution witnesses. Let us follow a certain order. Vahid Hajdarevic. With regard to this witness, it was not stated that the witness said that he was mistreated by HVO soldiers outside the Kaonik prison and not in the prison, which is relevant. Witness A. It has not been mentioned, though the witness did say this, that he was brought to Kaonik by the HVO military police on the 24th of January, 1993, and that at the time he did not see Zlatko Aleksovski but that he saw him only three or four days later when he replaced the commander. It is true that the Prosecution mentions in three places in the indictment that Zlatko Aleksovski, sometime about the 29th of January, arrived in the Kaonik prison. If we know that the first clashes and the first detentions and the bringing in of prisoners to Kaonik occurred on the 24th and the 25th of January, then the conclusion that is self-evident is that when he arrived in Kaonik, Zlatko Aleksovski found a situation such as it was over which he had no influence, and this is a point that I wish to underline as being extremely significant. That witness -- I am still talking about Witness A -- explicitly said that, according to his understanding, Zlatko Aleksovski had no influence over the HVO soldiers and the military policemen who were the prison guards. He also said that in connection with the unfortunate murder of two Bosnian Muslims that occurred on the 7th of February, 1993, an investigation was started. He also said that a physician from Busovaca would come to Kaonik. Most important of all, and which is indicative of his attitude towards Zlatko Aleksovski, he said that after all those war events, which were by no means easy to live through for members of either ethnic groups, the Bosniak Muslims and the Bosnian Croats, he said that Zlatko Aleksovski came to his house, that they had a cup of coffee, that they ate cake, which is indicative of his judgement of Zlatko Aleksovski's behaviour in Kaonik during those unfortunate events. Witness B was brought to Kaonik also by the HVO, the military police, on the 25th of January. According to his own testimony, he had two grenades and a pistol on him. I am drawing your attention to this fact because, through the testimony of a Prosecution witness, it confirms the position of the Defence as to the reason why Bosnian Muslim civilians were detained in the former military barracks in Kaonik. I am referring to their security. I will explain this later, but please bear this in mind, though, of course, I will remind you of this when the time comes. So this witness had on him two grenades and a pistol, according to his own admission. In the case of Witness B, he had a Zolja -- I don't know whether you know what a Zolja is. I'm not a military expert, but it is a weapon used in anti-tank combat, so it's a very powerful weapon. He also said that he was taken by the military police to Kaonik to dig trenches and that they had dug trenches during the daytime, and that if it was dangerous, they would dig at night. Witness F. That witness, according to his own admission, also had a weapon, an automatic pistol called a Skorpio. I remind you again of that question of security as being the reason for detention. However, Witness F, like Witnesses G, O, and S, did not identify Zlatko Aleksovski in this courtroom as the person who was the warden of the military prison in Kaonik at the critical time. This is another illustration of the relevance of the statements made by Prosecution witnesses. Witness L said that he went to see a doctor in Busovaca at his own request, that he was mistreated by members of the military police before he reached Kaonik at a locality called Kace. However, in spite of this, there is no record in medical documentation of him having sustained any injuries. Witness N also spoke about poor conditions in Kaonik, but he said that talking to the Red Cross, which he had on his own, that he made no complaints as regards the poor conditions or any injuries that he may have sustained. Edin Novalic is one of the significant witnesses who, before the unfortunate events in Busovaca municipality, was a very important person. He was the manager of a large economic facility. He mixed in political circles and with people who, in the former Yugoslavia, held certain positions, and after the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina gained independence, they again held positions of authority. So he, like Fuad Kaknjo, Bahtija Sivro, also Prosecution witnesses, mixed in circles and with people who held positions linked to the authorities and to decision-making important for that community. Nowhere, never, has any one of those witnesses seen Zlatko Aleksovski, which shows that Zlatko Aleksovski did not participate in any bodies which made any decisions one way or the other, and so he did not participate in decision-making regarding events that were a consequence of the acts mentioned in the indictment because the indictment charges Aleksovski with participating in the planning, instigation, and acts which resulted in the armed conflict in the territory of Busovaca municipality. However, there was no evidence, not a single piece of evidence, to corroborate this allegation in the course of these proceedings. Witness Meho Sivro also stated that he was mistreated by HVO soldiers outside of Kaonik and that he even asked to be returned to Kaonik because he felt safe there, safer than he was on the front lines where he was a member of the labour detachment working on fortifications. Many witnesses who referred to alleged mistreatment in the Kaonik facility said that they personally had not seen such mistreatment. They said they heard sounds. Some of them even said that they thought it was over the radio, over the loudspeaker. It is worth mentioning the example of Witness E, Your Honours, who, in his testimony -- which was not quoted by the Prosecutor but I will do so -- said that he gave to a guard in Kaonik 10.000 German marks, which was an enormous sum in those days, and it still is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, to look after them for him because he had that money on him as he was going to purchase material. When he was released from Kaonik, that same guard returned that same sum of money to him. This is also illustrative of many things. Similarly, many detainees working in those labour detachments, were, in fact, mistreated and robbed by HVO soldiers, which just shows that when they came to Kaonik, they were allowed to keep their valuables, watches, and so on. As one of the objective pieces of evidence that I referred to a moment ago, I should like to remind Your Honours of Defence Exhibits D23 and D24 which are documents of the International Red Cross, including photographs taken in Kaonik. If you look at those photographs, you will see that the detainees on the photographs are decently dressed, that they are wearing jewellery, gold chains, watches, that you cannot see on any one of them any trace of injury. This is something that the Defence considers to be objective proof because, after all, cameras cannot lie. Witness Fuad Kaknjo is one of the persons who is on the photograph that has been admitted as Exhibit D24 and who was recognised by Defence witness Zeljko Percinlic. Please look at that photograph and you will see that that person is not starved nor is he injured, even though some witnesses claimed that he was injured and that he had bruises on his face. Witness Bahtija Sivro was also one of the more prominent figures in the municipality, and he was the one, when armed conflicts broke out between the Bosnian Muslims and Croats, who tried to intervene. In what way? By calling up the commander of the BH army, Ramiz Dugalic, on the telephone, and telling him that the BH army should cease its offensive operations. Those are the words he used, "offensive operations." Mr. Meddegoda quoted Prosecution witnesses, who said that they had seen Croatian soldiers, in arguing the existence of an international conflict. However, we must understand what the witnesses are talking about. When a witness mentions Croatian soldiers, they are referring to Bosnian Croats in the HVO and not to Croatian citizens from the Republic of Croatia. So, for example, the quoted witness Daniel Damon, a freelance journalist who was working for Sky Television and who travelled all over Bosnia, said explicitly when asked that never in the territory of Busovaca or Central Bosnia had he seen a single HV soldier, a soldier of the Croatian army, only in Tomislavgrad, which is an area removed from this, much closer to the southern border of the Republic of Croatia, closer to Dalmacija, that only there did he see a bus with licence plates of the Croatian army. The same holds true of Mr. Torbjorn Junhov and Mr. Charles McLeod who were officials of the International Red Cross or members of the European Monitors, when asked said that they had never seen soldiers of the Croatian army in the area of Central Bosnia. That is what they said. However, attention should be drawn to the testimony of Mr. Hamdo Dautovic that my learned friend quoted in a rather significant context. Let us recall the testimony of Hamdo Dautovic. As this was quite some time ago, allow me to remind you of the key points. Witness Hamdo Dautovic was arrested at a checkpoint of the military police of the HVO, and in his car, a large quantity of cigarettes was found. At the time, cigarettes were a rare commodity in Central Bosnia, and these were products for smuggling and black marketeering. According to his statement, Dautovic had purchased these cigarettes, and he tried to smuggle them into the area where he had resided. According to his own admission, he was arrested for the criminal offence of smuggling, which is a criminal offence according to any legislation in the world. He resisted arrest by starting a fight with a military policeman, by jumping out of a speeding car, by trying to snatch a rifle from a military policeman, and when the Defence asked him why, he said "In order to kill them." Of course, when resisting arrest, jumping from a moving car, attempting to seize a rifle, physical force was used, and, of course, on that occasion, Hamdo Dautovic would have received blows as a result of this incident. All this shows that this was a typical case of policing and that Hamdo Dautovic cannot be compared with persons who were brought to Kaonik as interned civilians from Busovaca and the surroundings on two occasions. This was a police arrest. He is in a solitary cell, he said that himself, so that he cannot in any way compare with others. That is one side of the argument. The other is that the Defence believes that his testimony with respect to the mistreatment he was exposed to is absolutely untrustworthy. The Defence does not believe a single word the witness said in this context. Let me explain. According to his own story, he spent 30 days in Kaonik. Each day within that period, he was allegedly seriously physically mistreated. Even on the last day, when he was released on the 19th of June, 1993, again, he was beaten up. And what happened? Hamdo Dautovic got into a bus. The bus takes him to Zenica, the closest large city under the control of the BH army and inhabited predominantly by Bosniak Muslims. He goes to the hospital there to seek medical treatment. For 30 days, he was continuously physically abused. In the hospital, nothing happens. After his admission to the hospital, he spent the night there because he came in the evening, and in the morning, after being examined, he is discharged and sent home. There is no hospital in the world with a person physically beaten up with numerous injuries, according to his testimony, that would discharge him from the hospital in Zenica in a territory controlled by his own ethnic group. That is simply impossible. To that, Hamdo Dautovic, according to his own statement, was treated by applying lambskins to his body. This testimony indicates a conclusion of the Defence or perhaps a position taken by the Defence, and that is that the Defence considers that the testimonies of the Prosecution witnesses, who said that they were seriously physically maltreated in Kaonik camp, should not be believed. Let me explain why. If we go back to the beginning and what I said when I started my statement, that truth, like art, is in the eyes of the beholder, then you will understand me when I say to you that those witnesses are perhaps telling a subjective truth, what they believe to be true, but I consider that that subjective truth that they are uttering in no way is objectively verified. If I say, Your Honours, for example, that I hit myself and that I have a lot of pain, perhaps that is what I feel, but the level of tolerance of my pain and the threshold of tolerance of somebody else is different, and whether the injury sustained is an injury in the medical sense or not, that is a question that must be objectively verified. What way are we going to do this? The only way that it can be objectively verified, that is to say, an injury to physical integrity, is to have a medical examination performed. The physician must examine the individual in question and must say what injury has been sustained. He must describe the injury. If it is a question of fractures of any kind, then x-rays must be performed, and so on and so forth. Why? Not only are we then confronted with a scientific approach and assessment and evaluation of the fact which is decisive for a ruling in this instance, but that fact later on can be subjected to scrutiny to determine whether it is trustworthy or not by an expert witness, a forensic expert. That is precisely the individual who can tell us what it is all about, that is to say, the degree of the injury, whether it is a light injury, a serious injury, one that can be life threatening perhaps. That is the individual competent, with all his scientific knowledge, to tell us how the injury was incurred and sustained, the mechanism which caused it. Once we have evidence treated in this way, we can say that we have treated it objectively and examined it objectively. I'm quite certain that the legal standards of this Trial Chamber are extremely high without any doubt. However, I will say that a minimum legal standard in criminal procedure in the country where I come, that is to say, from the area of the former Yugoslavia, from Croatia, is the following: You cannot accuse somebody of having inflicted serious bodily injury if the injury has not been verified in the manner that I have described. Similarly, it is not possible, I suppose, to convict somebody of murder without having a dead body. Those then are some legal standards inherent in criminal law which I consider to be absolutely applicable in this case as well because, and this is a point that I think we will all agree upon, here we are applying and we wish to establish individual criminal liability, that of Mr. Aleksovski. As that is so, then we can apply all of the legal standards which have been well founded in the criminal codes of the countries in question. Witness K, who was mentioned by my learned colleague from the Prosecution, in his testimony told the Court -- he showed the Court two maps, and on those maps, he indicated the positions of the BH army and the positions of the HVO in the area of the Busovaca municipality and further afield in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This piece of evidence is also highly indicative because, with an overview, a scant overview of the indicated positions of the BH army with regard to the Busovaca municipality, which is the subject of this indictment, we can see at superficial glance that that area found itself in a strong encirclement by the BH army, and no paths led out of that encirclement.
