This fact, as well as the fact that Witness K spoke about, and that is the relationship of forces, the ratio of forces and manpower and human potential of both armies, that is to say, the BH army and the HVO army, was in the ratio of 5:1 or 8:1 to the advantage of the BH army. These facts, this complete encirclement, this visible predominance of the number of soldiers indicates that the Busovaca municipality area was truly and definitely under an encirclement. Therefore, this tells us a great deal about a fact that is quite opposite to the assertions made by the Prosecution, that is to say, that the Bosnian Croats were organised in the HVO army and they unleashed a process of attacking Bosniak Muslims in the Busovaca municipality. That is quite simply, to even a military layman, evident at first glance, that is to say, that somebody who finds himself in an encirclement and who is numerically weaker in a ratio of 5:1 or 8:1 will not be capable of attacking. As I say, these are all details, details which the Prosecution witnesses spoke about and which the Prosecution understands in a different light but which I feel to be absolutely relevant, and, Your Honours, you must bear this in mind. Mr. Meddegoda mentioned, in the context of establishing an international armed conflict, the testimony by expert witness Professor Bianchini. I am going to refer to what Professor Bianchini, the expert witness, said later on in my presentation when I come to speak about the key moments which the Defence considers to be important for judgement, and that is the application of law and the international armed conflict; next, the issue of serious breaches of the Geneva Conventions, violations as envisaged by the Statute of this Tribunal in Article 3. Next, when we speak of the international armed conflict, in a way, but not directly as Professor Bianchini discussed the point, I must return to yesterday's closing argument by my learned colleague, Mr. Niemann, who spoke about that point. I must say that I was surprised with regard to some of the assertions made and articulated by my learned colleague with regard to the application of law and certain standards. The thesis of the Prosecution is that Article 2 of the Statute of this Tribunal need not necessarily be applied to an international conflict but that it can be applied to an internal conflict as well. In the arguments put forward to support that thesis, our distinguished colleague, the Prosecutor, speaks in the direction of the following, that is, that this Trial Chamber must bear in mind the new trends in articulating this entire issue which were presented in certain decisions taken by this Tribunal. This thesis is untenable in the view of the Defence, and it is untenable for two reasons: The first reason is that this Tribunal applies international customary law, not to speak of the Geneva Conventions and The Hague Protocols, which are a source of law for the Tribunal, but the Tribunal, in addition to these sources, also incontestably applies international customary law. The Secretary-General of the U.N. Security Council indicates in his letter, I think it was the letter of the 3rd of May, 1993 to the Security Council, and he pointed this out when the Statute of this Tribunal was put up for adoption. Therefore, this Tribunal has the authority of applying the legal standards which existed and, I emphasise, are an incontestable part of international customary law. The decisions brought up and indicated by Mr. Niemann are not contested as international -- they are not international customary law. Perhaps they will become so in three, four, five years, but they are not, and that is the first reason. The second reason is that, with this kind of approach, the application of a new development of law would de facto violate the principle which we all know from ancient Roman law, which is one of the basic principles, and that is nullum crimen sine lege, nulla poena sine lege. We cannot apply -- I say we cannot --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, perhaps you should slow down because I think that our court reporters do not know Latin, so they were not able to catch the phrase that you used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I shall repeat. I said that this thesis is in opposition to the principle of Roman law nullum cremin sine lege, nulla poena sine lege. I am sure that I need not explain the meaning of that phrase because you know it much better than I do myself, but I think that it is a key element within which we must revolve when selecting law principles in this case. As the Blaskic decision, in rejecting the proposal put forward by the Trial Chamber that certain points in the indictment linked to an international armed conflict be refuted -- so the Blaskic decision, and it was Trial Chamber I that took the decision -- was that the question of an international conflict was a combined legal and factual issue which must be ascertained during the proceedings. That is what we ascertained and established in the course of these proceedings. Therefore, it is the position of the Defence, and the Defence's position is quite the opposite to the Prosecution, and that is that Article 2 of the Statute exclusively and only can be applied to an international armed conflict. In that regard, the Defence would like to point out the decision taken in the Tadic case, Trial Chamber I, because that is the sole decision which at this point in time with regard to this question has a foundation in law and is in effect. Furthermore, going back to the closing argument of my distinguished colleague, the Defence must note that some assertions seem to us not to correspond to the situation as it is, and we cannot agree with the statement and assertion that the Prosecution need not necessarily prove but that some things can be intimated. This is something that the Defence cannot agree with and that the Defence considers is not a standard which should be applied by this Honorary Tribunal. Of course, the classification of an armed conflict has nothing to do with the crimes committed. I completely agree on that point with my learned colleague. However, the classification of an armed conflict does have absolute value when the law is applied and when the competencies of the Court come into question. I have in mind this Tribunal as opposed to the competencies of national courts. Of course, there I agree with Mr. Niemann as well, that the Geneva Conventions did not foresee an International Tribunal of this type because it was not in existence. However, the Tribunal by adopting the Statute took on the Geneva Conventions as a source of law and all the other sources that we mentioned, The Hague Protocols and incontestable international customary law. That Tribunal, with the decision that I mentioned a moment ago from the Tadic Appeals Chamber, expressly stated that Article 2 of the Statute can be applied only in events within the frameworks of an international armed conflict. Contrary to the position of the Prosecution, the Defence considers that it is precisely this question, the question of an international armed conflict, that is the essential question and issue for defining a criminal act which is the subject of this trial, because this is not only a legal matter, but it is also a factual matter. Our learned colleague, the Prosecutor, went on to speak about command responsibility and referred to Article 7 of the Statute, and, whether consciously or inadvertently, he said, and I quote: "Zlatko Aleksovski did not have full power or complete authority." Now, does that statement made by our learned colleague mean in a way recognition of certain positions taken by the Defence or not? We shall see in due course, but that is how we have experienced it, either there is authority or there is not any authority or an absence of authority. I agree with the thesis put forward by the Prosecution that command responsibility is not exclusively applicable in military structures but that it can be applied to civilians as well. However, there is a great "but" here, "but" with a capital "B," and that is what category of civilian are we dealing with? What category of civilian can perform a function within a command responsibility? Let me remind you of some examples from court practice, recent court practice, where we are exclusively dealing with highly positioned civilian officials such as a defence minister, the mayors of towns, governors. Those are individuals who are so high on the hierarchical ladder in the civilian echelons of power and authority, that by virtue of their position and authority, they come under command -- this implies command responsibility. But if we go back to the positions of my defendant, Mr. Aleksovski, and if we go back to the statements made by witnesses in this courtroom, then we shall recall that nobody, none of the witnesses placed Zlatko Aleksovski at any highly ranked civilian post. I have in mind the municipal structures of power and authority and other structures of power and authority making important decisions for the area in which they were made and in which the events took place, the events mentioned in the indictment. On this occasion, Mr. Niemann referred to the case, the U.S.A. against Oswald Pohl. However, the Defence feels that this precedent cannot be applied to the concrete case in point because we are dealing with an event from another environment, from an international armed conflict, and because the protected individuals in the camp commanded by Oswald Pohl had quite a different status than did the individuals who were detained in the Kaonik camp. The Defence maintains, and it will expound this later on, that the Bosniak Muslims who were interned in the Kaonik camp had the position of internees, according to the Second Hague Protocol which is the law applying to that situation and not the position of prisoners according to the Geneva Conventions of 1949, and that is a great difference. The Defence will elaborate and expound on that point later on. The importance and position of my defendant, Mr. Aleksovski -- let me say that the Prosecution tells of the killing of two Bosniak Muslims on the 7th of February, 1993, Nermin Elezovic and Jasmin Sehovic. This was brought up by the Prosecutor. The Prosecution states as follows: "Mr. Aleksovski had all the power because he undertook an investigation against the perpetrators of that criminal act ..." However, the Prosecution forgets a very important situation which is envisaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think that if we are going to work until 1.00, it will be a very long period of work. I don't know whether perhaps it would suit you to have a short break of 15 minutes and then we can resume after that. Otherwise, we can finish before 1.00. But I think it would be preferable to have a 15-minute break, and I am saying this so that Mr. Aleksovski can also leave the courtroom. So we are now going to have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may continue up to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I continue with my argument -- and this is a point addressed to the interpreters -- when I mention persons that are interned in the Kaonik camp, would those terms be used, "internment" and "internees," because I consider this to be a key issue that is very important point from the standpoint of law. Not "detainees," not "prisoners," but "internees." Thank you. Let me go back to where I stopped. We were discussing the tragic event of the 7th of February, 1993, when, while engaging in forced labour on the front lines, two Bosniak Muslims were killed, Nermin Elezovic and Jasmin Sehovic. We heard testimony about this, as to how this had happened and where it had happened, so quite clearly outside the Kaonik facility, and we also heard -- and this is something that the Defence has corroborated with exhibits that have been admitted into evidence as D22A and B -- immediately after this tragic event, Mr. Aleksovski reacted by informing the military police about the event. The military police conducted an investigation, a police investigation, and arrested the suspects, and, after that, handed the case over to the military prosecutor's office which, in turn, the military prosecutor's office submitted a request for court proceedings to the competent court. This is a procedure which is prescribed by the National Code on Criminal Procedure. The role of Mr. Aleksovski in this event is the role that every citizen has in the territory of the former Yugoslavia in which the law on criminal procedure is applied. This means that, should any citizen have any knowledge about the commission of a criminal offence, especially of such a grave crime, it is his civil duty to inform the police of the same. In such a situation, the citizen, in this case Mr. Aleksovski as well, has the role of a completely informal reporter of the event. Only when that information about a crime that has been committed reaches the police does the normal part of the procedure begin as stipulated by the law: The police conducts the investigation, it identifies the perpetrator and hands them over to the courts. Therefore, Mr. Aleksovski, in this event, had no other role than that of an honest and conscientious citizen who, on the basis of his own conscience, reported the crime to the competent body for such proceedings, in this case to the military police. I do not know, Your Honours, how this matter is dealt with or regulated in the national legislations of the countries you come from, but I do know that, for instance, the national legislation of the United States of America authorises the citizen to even arrest the perpetrator of a criminal offence, which is known as "civil arrest." Therefore, what Zlatko Aleksovski did is nothing unusual, it is quite customary, at least in the area that Mr. Aleksovski comes from, and that is the area of the former Yugoslavia. Therefore, the act of Zlatko Aleksovski should not be viewed in the way it is viewed by the Prosecution; it should not be seen as indicative of any elements of command responsibility but solely as elements of civil conscientious behaviour. Mr. Aleksovski, of course, is here in this Tribunal charged with very grave offences and, as is appropriate when reviewing such serious cases, I too, in this case, have been giving thought to the question of motive. What was it that prompted the potential perpetrator, in this case Mr. Aleksovski, to commit a criminal offence? The Prosecution has touched upon this issue by saying that it has been clearly proven in the proceedings that Zlatko Aleksovski, and I quote, "was a supporter of the Croatian cause," and the Croatian cause, according to the allegations of the Prosecution, was to ethnically cleanse Central Bosnia in spite of the encirclement, the numerical superiority, et cetera, that we have discussed. Your Honours, if Zlatko Aleksovski is a supporter of the Croatian cause and demonstrates this by being the son of a mixed marriage -- his father was a Macedonian, therefore not a Croat, he married a woman of Serb ethnicity -- he spent most of his life in Zenica surrounded mostly, or in 80 per cent of the cases, by citizens of Muslim ethnicity, that his closest friends were Muslims, I really have to ask myself: Where does the Prosecution find the grounds to allege that Zlatko Aleksovski is a supporter of the Croatian cause? This merely shows that Zlatko Aleksovski was a person without any national or religious prejudices. So much, at this point, as far as motive is concerned. Referring to the closing argument of my learned friend, Mr. Niemann, the Defence would like to state the following: We do not believe and feel that it has not been proven that the quoted witnesses spoke about their suffering in a manner that can be objectively applied to the legal standards of this Tribunal. We can understand and we do understand, without any reservation, their bitterness on account of the events in Central Bosnia. These are people who, for various reasons which are far more complex than the reasons that the Prosecution has tried to elucidate, were forced to abandon their homes, places where they had spent their youth, had their property, these were people that have every reason to be bitter; and viewed from this standpoint, their testimony should be understood. I link this to the truth, that is, in the eyes of the beholder; therefore, the subjective truth. In his closing argument, Mr. Niemann frequently referred to the Celebici trial, and he tried to make some comparisons in fact and in law between the Aleksovski trial and the Celebici trial. The Defence is not inclined towards making any such comparisons or drawing any kind of analogy out of reasons of principle already because analogy is not allowed in criminal law, but also because this is a trial that is sub judice, the appeals procedure has not even started in the Celebici case but it has been announced. What the final ruling will be, what the position of the Appeals Chamber of this Tribunal will be, is yet to be seen. Any attempt to make any analogy and to refer to certain determinations, to certain facts which stem from the Celebici trial, is not seen as being trustworthy by the Defence. We feel that such analogy is out of place. It is the submission of the Defence that when selecting legal sources, in addition to The Hague and Geneva Conventions, I repeat, we need to apply, without question, customary law. Professor Bianchini, an expert witness called by the Prosecution to this courtroom with the idea in mind to provide Your Honours with more detailed explanations of the facts in the territory of the former Yugoslavia and specifically in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so that through his expert testimony, the state of an international armed conflict should be confirmed in the area covered by the indictment. Ninety or even more per cent of that testimony that we heard in the courtroom presented by Stefano Bianchini is accepted by the Defence. Some things will be disputed by the Defence, but by far the greatest part of that expert testimony is accepted by the Defence as being trustworthy and reliable and based on fact. It is undisputed -- I am referring to the testimony of Professor Stefano Bianchini -- that there is no doubt that in this unfortunate conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in this area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, never in history was there any conflict between the Bosniaks and the Muslims; on the contrary, they were allies. Historically, on the basis of historiography, this conflict was an isolated incident, a blemish on the historical map of events. The cause of the war in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, without any doubt, should be sought in the Serbian hegemony personified in the figure of Slobodan Milosevic who proclaimed, as his ideological basis, the well-known memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. That is something discussed by Professor Bianchini and that, in fact, was the cause of all these unfortunate events. As far as the problem that occurred in Bosnia is concerned, allow me to remind you, Your Honours, and to draw your attention to the beginning of those events. The International Community, from the very first, tried to resolve those relationships -- we are prone to call it "the Bosnian pot" -- by acting as mediators in trying to appease the situation and to find a solution to the inter-ethnic intolerance. This deserves praise, and this is something that all the peoples of the former Yugoslavia craved because, unfortunately, they couldn't come to an agreement themselves. How did this go? Let me remind Your Honours of the meeting held in March 1992 in the Konak Villa near Sarajevo, a meeting organised by the representative of the International Community, Mr. Cutiliero, and to which the following were invited: Mr. Boban as a representative of the Croatian people, Mr. Izetbegovic as a represent of the Muslim people, and Mr. Karadzic as a representative of the Serbian people in Bosnia. What was the fundamental conclusion of that meeting held in March 1992, Your Honours? The ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into a Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian pot. Bearing this in mind, and Prosecutor's Exhibit number 506 corroborates this, it was an ethnic map, bearing this in mind, we can rightly ask ourselves: What, in those days, did members of ethnic groups in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina believe, because that is the only solution, as that is what the International Community is telling us, that Bosnia should be divided up? I'm not saying that that was the main cause of the war and the fighting in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but it is quite certain that that too was one of the causes. I have already said in what respects I agree with Professor Bianchini, that the main cause was the Serbian hegemony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I think we have to stop there for a break, and we will resume work at 2.30. Thank you. Have a good lunch, everyone. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor. We're going to work more or less for one hour, ten minutes, after which we shall have a break. You may continue, Mr. Mikulicic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'll continue where I left off before the break, which was an interpretation, that is to say, commenting on the expert witness Professor Stefan Bianchini. For an introduction to what I'm going to say next, let me mention that I mentioned the meeting of March 1992 in the Villa Konak near Sarajevo, a meeting organised by the International Community as the monitor, in an attempt to resolve the Bosnian crisis and which, in fact, resulted with a proposal for the ethnic division of Bosnia into a Serbian, Muslim, and Croatian section, and as was shown on the map which was tendered into evidence, and it was P116, Prosecution Exhibit. After that, Professor Bianchini informed us of the fact that the same idea was present in the so-called Vance-Owen Plan, and with this, the fact was highlighted that the International Community at that time attempted to resolve the Bosnian question in the way that Bosnia should be divided among the majority nations living in that country. Later on, that approach was left behind, was given up, and we are witnesses that, after the Dayton Peace Agreements, the International Community took over the thesis of a unified Bosnia. However, the harm that was caused by this kind of clumsy, if I may say so, mentorship of the International Community in 1992, I'm afraid, for a long time will not be able to put right, incorrigible, for a long time to come. Although it is not the principal reason, it is one of the reasons for the war in Bosnia, a policy of this kind. Now, why am I saying this? I'm saying this because I want to show the confrontations that ensued in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to remind you of what I said this morning, that conflicts were not simple, and that in Bosnia, everybody fought against everybody in the different parts of Bosnia. Professor Bianchini, in his expert testimony, referred to the book by Croatian General Janko Bobetko, which was published recently in the Republic of Croatia. In the book, the book contains his orders on the deployment of the units of the Croatian army on the territory of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, of course, with the idea of demonstrating that what we're dealing with was an international armed conflict because the army of the Republic of Croatia, that is to say, one sovereign State, intervened in the area of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, another sovereign State. When you assess this evidence, I should like to ask you to bear in mind these key factors: First, all the documents date back to 1992, that is to say, they refer to the period which is outside the frameworks of the incriminations in the indictment that we are discussing in this trial. Second, all the documents refer to the activities of the Croatian army in the area of Herzegovina and the border region of the southern battlefield of the Republic of Croatia and Posavina, this border area of the Slovenian front. Third, to a direct question, Professor Bianchini answered the following when directly asked: That the enemy mentioned in these military orders is the Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say, the JNA, that is to say, the Serbian and Montenegrin paramilitary formations. What does that mean? That means that the units of the Croatian army in the border regions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were not fighting against the Muslim units or against the Muslim population, but together with the units of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they were fighting against an enemy, an aggressor, that is to say, the former Yugoslav People's Army, that is to say, the Serbian and Montenegrin paramilitary formations. Also, Professor Bianchini, when directly asked, answered the following: He said that at the critical time, no conflicts between the Bosniak Muslims and Croats existed. Therefore, this presence of the units of the Croatian army in the border regions of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in no way whatsoever can be linked with the events in Central Bosnia. First, because they took place at quite a different time; second, because they took place in quite a different area. In order to clarify matters, the presence of the units of the Croatian army on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time, Professor Bianchini indicates, upon the insistence of the Defence, on the agreement signed by the presidents of two sovereign States, the Republic of Croatia on the one side and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the other, Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic, once again in 1992, which, among others -- that is to say, the agreement of friendship and cooperation which, among others, envisages cooperation on a military level. The other witnesses brought forward by the Prosecution only indirectly spoke about this question, and I should like to indicate the testimony of Mr. Charles McLeod, Junhov Torbjorn who, as European Monitors, that is to say, officials of the International Red Cross, were in a position constantly to be on the terrain and to view the situation from there. They never saw the presence of the Croatian army in Central Bosnia in the Busovaca area. Just in the way that Professor Bianchini, the Prosecution witness, and the Prosecution tried to give a better understanding of relations in the region through him, so did the Defence bring forward an expert witness, he was Professor Bilandzic who, in a very transparent and translucent way, in exact terms, explained the precise reasons for the disintegration of the former Yugoslavia. What, in fact, happened in that regard? I am not going to tire you by bringing up once again the things he said in his testimony. I should just like to remind you of his basic thesis as an expert in the field, as a historiographer, that, in fact, parallel with the processes of creating Yugoslavia, that is to say, from 1918 onwards, parallel with this integrative process, at the same time, we had a disintegrative process going on. At some points in time, one would be dominant or the other, the balance of scales would tip, but all this was to lead to the end it led to, which, if we look at it from the historiographical standpoint, was the only possible outcome from the situation as it was. Your Honours, the Defence would now like to comment and refer to several key situations which are the subject of the indictment. I have already said something by way of introduction. Let me just repeat briefly what I said on this occasion. The question that is raised is whether or not Mr. Aleksovski, with relation to the position he held, had the kind of authority and competence, that he could use his authority and competence on the basis of which we conclude his command responsibility. It has not been disputed in this case that at the critical time, Mr. Aleksovski performed the function of warden of the military prison of Kaonik. In a situation of this kind, evidence has shown that Mr. Aleksovski came to the Kaonik facility, which had previously been adapted for the purposes of forming a military prison sometime at the end of January or the beginning of February 1993. This is a fact that the indictment operates with, and the 29th of January is a date that is mentioned as the date when he came to the Kaonik facility. Evidence showed that Mr. Aleksovski was a civilian. He was not a member of the HVO. He was not a member of the military police either. He did not have a rank. He did not have any military functions. This was borne out, both by Prosecution and Defence witnesses. Numerous Prosecution witnesses said that Mr. Aleksovski did not have any authorisation vis-à-vis the soldiers of the military police, who were the guards in the facility and who were located not very far from the prison in a separate building next to the entrance itself. The question arises as to what kind of competence and authorisation Mr. Aleksovski had in the military prison of Kaonik. It is not disputed, therefore, that he was a civilian and that the guards were military personnel, military policemen. Both theoretically and practically, it is rather dubious whether a civilian can issue orders to military men. The Defence maintains that Zlatko Aleksovski, in performing the function of warden of the prison, only had exclusively administrative powers and authorisation to have contacts with the representatives of international organisations which visited the Kaonik facility, the Red Cross, the European Monitors, the members of some other civic or humanitarian associations. From that authorisation that he had, we cannot draw the conclusion that that authorisation represents the essence of his command responsibility. For us to be able to see whether the command responsibility exists or not with regard to the military police in the person of Mr. Aleksovski, my client, we must understand one thing, and that is that the military police was a formation which had its own commander, and the commander, according to military hierarchy, once again had his superior. Nobody outside that structure of the military police, that is to say, the army, had the authorisation to issue orders to soldiers in the sense that within full scope he was able to use his command responsibility. When I say that, I mean the following, that is to say, the possibility of control over the execution of an order and sanctions if orders were not carried out. If these two components are lacking, then, Your Honours, there is no question of command responsibility. That would be command responsibility of a declarative nature and not of an essential nature. It is important to note that Mr. Aleksovski, and this was borne out by many witnesses, did not have the authorisation to punish military policemen if they failed to obey or if they failed in their conduct in any way or for anything else. The Defence does not claim that the question of command responsibility should exclusively be viewed within the context of a military organisation; the Defence allows for the possibility of a civilian individual also coming under the notion of command responsibility. But, Your Honours, only in exceptional cases and only with regard to that civilian who is ranked sufficiently high up on the hierarchy of power and authority so that through the force of his position he is able to issue binding orders to military personnel. In the structure of today's society as we know it, this would be, for example, Defence Ministers who, in democratic systems, are civilians. Another example would be the governors of individual regions, perhaps even mayors, but, in any case, individuals who, in the civilian hierarchy, are placed extremely high, top level. If you remember the evidence presented before you, not a single piece of evidence leads us to conclude that Mr. Aleksovski performed any type of high civilian post of this kind. He was not a member even of the municipal authorities of the small town of Busovaca, let alone any other top-level civilian political body. Similarly, Mr. Aleksovski was not a member of any negotiating commissions, expert bodies for exchange for detainees or internees. Mr. Aleksovski never was seen by any of the witnesses at any single meeting of civilian individuals discussing important topics, and we say this with full responsibility when we say that the question of command responsibility of a civilian in this concrete case cannot be implied as being embodied in Mr. Aleksovski. Therefore, what remains for us? The fact remains that as the warden of a military prison, Mr. Aleksovski could have been in charge of administrative affairs, that is to say, which guard will do what shift or how many meals will be served per day for the needs of the prisoners or internees, how many meals a day should be cooked, or to decide other matters related to the functioning of the prison itself in this purely administrative sense of governing the prison. True authorisation, as to issuing permits, for example, allowing access to Kaonik for the interned individuals or dismissing, releasing them, or prisoners, permits for this, in the form of disciplinary action or sanctions, Mr. Aleksovski did not have authorisation of that kind. This was borne out by the president of the municipal district court in Travnik who, in his testimony, explained to us the relationship towards Zlatko Aleksovski and Zlatko Aleksovski's relationship towards other relevant bodies of the powers that be at the time. However, what Mr. Aleksovski could have done is he could complain about certain excesses that had taken place, he could have reported to the competent bodies conduct which was against the law, and that is what he, in fact, did. Let us go back to the case of Sehovic and Elezovic, that killing, and let me remind you of the documented evidence which the Defence presented as Defence Exhibits 21 A, B, and C, and also other substantiated evidence, D25 and D26, Defence Exhibits 25 and 26, and they are written documents which Mr. Aleksovski sent to the military district court in Travnik, that is to say, to the commander of the military units, for him to react with regard to conduct on the part of the military policemen, contrary to the law, who resorted to the use of force -- who entered forcibly the prison without having a permit to do so. I should like Your Honours to recall Mr. Junhov's evidence. He wanted to visit the Kaonik facility and asked permission to do so, and permission for him to do so was issued by the police, not by Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski, because Mr. Zlatko Aleksovski was not authorised to issue a permit allowing individuals to visit the prison. This is just giving you a rough idea of the competences that he had in view of his position. I should also like to remind you, Your Honours, that, in this case, a recurring topic is the fact that from the prison, interned Bosniak Muslims were taken out and sent to do forced labour, trench-digging, fortifications, and so on, and that that fact is said to be a crime that Mr. Aleksovski committed, in taking these people out to do this forced labour. In the area of Busovaca, there were two ongoing conflicts, that is to say, the first began at the end of the month, it was a Sunday, the 24th of January, and the second took place in mid January, also in 1993. In these two periods, in the Kaonik facility, the population of Busovaca and the surrounding villages were interned. Who interned these individuals? Who brought them to Busovaca? Who ordered that they be taken there? We have not been able to ascertain that fact. In the course of the hearing, the Prosecution nor the Defence provided any evidence which would answer the question as to who issued the order for individuals to be interned in the Kaonik facility. However, one thing that is certain is that that order was not issued by Zlatko Aleksovski quite simply because he was not in a position to do so. He was not in a position to issue orders of that kind. By saying so, I do not wish to say that Mr. Aleksovski, as an individual who was to take care of administrative matters in the military prison of Kaonik, was, beside his own will, brought into a situation in which he attempted, through his professional involvement, to make it easier, to make the humanitarian situation better, and this situation was not, of course, ideal. I am going to speak later on about the legal foundations for the internment of Bosniak Muslims on that occasion, but I should just like to draw your attention for one moment to questions of command responsibility. Your Honours, let me remind you of the well-known decision taken by the tribunal for war crimes in Nuremberg in the case of the U.S.A. against Wilhelm von Leeb, it was known as "the high-command case," and it was the touchstone for laying the foundations for the responsibility of a commander, and it lays the groundwork and foundation for responsibility of this kind in the following way: You cannot find a commander guilty for the actions committed by his subordinates without having first determined the responsibility of these individuals. If we were to do so here, it would be to use a standard which is much below the standard of the international law used today. In other words, criminal responsibility of any individual has to be determined on a separate, individual basis. Your Honours, the authorities, that is, the legal sources with respect to military commanders are different from those that concern civilian individuals. We have the national and international basis of the law. So an accused who is not a military person is responsible for those actions in terms of his criminal responsibility which also are provided in the national law. So this would comprise murders, commission of serious bodily injury, rape, et cetera. Such criminal responsibility is not the same as the one provided for by the international law of war, and I believe that this is a perfectly clear distinction. What I am trying to say is that the military standard is much higher than the civilian standard, which is necessary in order to maintain a higher level of discipline and which then affects the superiors in order to maintain the military discipline. Article 7 of the Statute of this Tribunal provides the following: A crime has to have been committed by an individual who is a subordinate. The Statute asks whether the superior person was in a position to control the actions of his subordinate; in other words, whether the -- I think that the provisions about whether the commander had known or had a reason to know I think is perfectly clear. I am trying to point out that the commander has to have a possibility to control the actions of his subordinates, and I repeat "control," and that the actions of the subordinates have to appear within his own chain of responsibility. Your Honours, from the testimony of both the Prosecution and Defence witnesses, we saw that physical mistreatment, provided that it did happen, occurred outside of the Kaonik facility and was committed by persons who were not under the direct jurisdiction of Mr. Aleksovski, administrative jurisdiction of Mr. Aleksovski. Here he was operating as a civilian, and he reported to the competent authorities to further process the violations which he was aware of; but, Your Honours, Mr. Aleksovski had no authority to undertake any sanctions himself of the persons who had violated discipline, he had no such authority, and this authority does not issue from his duty. I have previously spoken about infliction of serious bodily injury and physical injury and great suffering to the detainees [interpretation error] in Kaonik. The Defence has presented a number of witnesses, including expert witnesses, medical staff from the health centre in Busovaca who have testified here, and we believe that their testimony was truthful and I think that important facts can be gathered from it. No one from the medical staff during the conflict, the period covered by the indictment, ever provided medical treatment to any seriously injured person who came from Kaonik, and serious injuries would include fractures, serious wounds, and such. Persons who came from Kaonik for medical care in Busovaca complained of chronic diseases, some acute diseases such as severe colds, stomach-ache and such. Your Honours, you have heard that despite assertions in the indictment that the hygienic conditions in Kaonik facility were below the minimum standard, no one from these individuals ever developed any contagious disease, none of the detainees [interpretation error] ever had any disease or complaint which developed from unhygienic conditions. Vesna Bilic, who was director of the health centre and who, by her position, was responsible for the implementation of the hygienic conditions in the entire area, testified that during this war period, no epidemic of any contagious disease was registered in the area or any other disease for that matter which may have been caused by lack of hygiene. The Defence considers this to be an objective fact and that in themselves they invalidate the allegation of poor hygienic conditions. It would have been impossible not to have some effects if the conditions were so poor. Also, had the physical abuse been so bad, some effect, some results, would have had to come from that, and we submit that these simply did not take place. So this short-term and temporary detention which took place on two occasions in Busovaca did not result in any serious decline in health conditions, and this should be taken as standard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention that Mr. Mikulicic said, for the record, that "internee" is the term to be used. I see here "temporary detention." I think that this correction needs to be made at the request of Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, you may continue. I think that was what you told us; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Thank you. I am grateful to the Trial Chamber for this intervention, and I again would like to request to interpret the Croatian word "internirani" with its English or French equivalent, which is "internment." Thank you. So, Your Honours, let me again repeat, we are talking about internees and internment, so let me address that issue right now. Unlike the position of the Prosecution, which somehow notoriously believes that internment of civilians in this critical period was something illegal, the Defence submits that there were sound legal reasons on the basis of international law to do so. The internment of civilians is not prohibited either by the Geneva Conventions or The Hague Protocols or international customary law. Of course, there are certain reservations and certain conventions within which such internment is permissible. In response to this query, let me, Your Honours, remind you of two court cases which have become authorities in this case as well. One of them is Korematsu versus the United States and Hirabayashi versus the United States. It refers to the events from 1942 on the west coast of the United States, in California. The local military commander declared, and the context was a war which had been declared between the United States and Japan, and he issued an order ordering that all U.S. citizens who were of Japanese origin who lived in that region were to be taken from their homes and gathered in collection centres, that is, that they should be interned. The reason for this decision was that a successful conduct of warfare also involves a prevention of any potential espionage against the U.S. government. In the case of Hirabayashi versus the U.S., the case was not as severe. U.S. citizens of Japanese origin were not taken to the collection centres and taken away from their homes but were placed under curfew. In other words, they were not permitted to leave their residences between 8.00 p.m. and 6.00 a.m. Both Mr. Hirabayashi and Mr. Korematsu have sued in order to challenge the legality of these decisions. The U.S. Congress and the Supreme Court of the United States took positions that they were not discriminated against and that the point of these decisions was its temporary nature for security reasons. If we are to view these cases in light of what happened in the Busovaca municipality area and in Kaonik, we can see that they are fully applicable. Moreover, it should be stressed that, at the time when these decisions were taken in the U.S., in the area where these decisions applied, there were no combat operations. The Japanese never reached California, and no combat operations were ever carried out in California, and, Your Honours, we saw what type of combat operations and war operations were conducted in the Busovaca area. Now, Your Honours, you have a situation where military conscripts, who are citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina and of Muslim ethnic background, are, in fact, staying in an area where the citizens of the Croatian ethnic origin are defending themselves from the attacks by the BH army. Your Honours, I would like to remind you of several examples where I said that certain Prosecution witnesses who had been interned in Kaonik had on them weapons and grenades and even anti-tank weapons. For Croats, the internment of the ethnic Muslims was a matter of security. I think we can agree that it was a temporary internment and short term. In the first case, it lasted between the 25th of January and the 6th of February; in the second instance, from the 16th or 17th of April until the end of May, at the latest. We can say that the interned persons, on average, spent up to two weeks in Kaonik. I agree that this too is too long. One day would have been too long under normal circumstances. Your Honours, at that time, in that place, the situation was terrible. You heard from witnesses. There was no place in the Busovaca municipality which had not been hit by a bullet, by a shell. Many civilians were killed by bullets or shells in their own homes. Nobody, not one person among the interned persons was injured or killed in the Kaonik facility. However, guards who guarded them did suffer injuries. One was injured in his genitals; another one was hit by shrapnel in the stomach in Kaonik itself where they were providing security for the facility. What is the point that I'm trying to make? I'm trying to point out that this issue of security as the reason for internment is twofold, and it should be interpreted from two points of view. One is the issue of internment, which is equivalent to the Korematsu and Hirabayashi cases; the second is the internment that coincides with the overall humanitarian situation. Because you will agree that it is better to have freedom of movement curbed and survive than not have any limits to the freedom of movement in the zone of combat operations and then be killed as a result of these combat operations. Finally, Your Honours, you should also bear in mind the fact, which is no less important, that any military units have to take special care of the civilians and forcibly remove them from the area of combat operations, and it is mandated by the Geneva Conventions to do so. When you view this issue in that light, I believe that you will be able to see these events of this unfathomable Bosnia in proper perspective. I repeat, however, that we haven't established who had ordered the internment; all we have established is that it was implemented by the military police of the HVO, but, as I said, the legal grounds for this can be very easily explained. Forced labour and the digging of trenches. This is another topic that we come across throughout the proceedings, and again, the a priori position of the Prosecution is that this is prohibited, that this is illegal, that there is nothing to be discussed. The Defence is of the opinion that that is not so. The Hague Protocol 2, which the Defence considers to be the authority in this particular case and which should be observed, says that internees may be used for forced labour on condition that they are working under similar conditions as the local civilian population. I think that I have almost literally quoted this provision of the Hague Protocol. What does this mean? This means that in the relevant period in the territory of Busovaca municipality, the provisions of local national legislation were applied which regulated forced labour. In this context, the Defence tendered into evidence the legislation that was in force at the time and which regulated forced labour. Those are Exhibits D28 and D28A. These are decrees regulating the obligation to work based on national legislation, and it says -- I don't wish to tire you with this -- but basically it says that during war, for the needs of combat operations and other needs of the armed forces, the organisation of work units may be ordered and that that order shall be issued by military officers in the event that the civilian authorities are not operational. Such work units may be organised to perform activities involved in the construction of fortifications, shelters, and other works of importance for defence. Your Honours, that is precisely what happened in the relevant period. Please recall the testimony of the witnesses. Military commanders of the HVO, on certain segments of the front lines, when they felt that they needed to fortify, to dig in, would send military policemen to form such work units, to bring them there, and for those units to carry out those works upon orders and under the command of the military commander in question. The Defence has called witnesses, citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina of non-Muslim ethnicity, a Serb with BH citizenship, and a Croat with BH citizenship who testified and confirmed that military policemen came to them, ordered them to come with them to the front line where they had to do forced labour. These were persons, men who were fit for military service in terms of age but who, for certain reasons, did not have weapons. Those men had to contribute to the joint defence effort in another way and not with weapons. Similarly, Your Honours, Bosnian Muslim civilians interned in Kaonik were also military conscripts, and there was absolutely no reason why those persons, like the non-internees, should not be used for forced labour, and they were indeed used and under similar conditions as the non-interned civilians. The military police participated in the implementation. They were taken to positions where the local commanders gave them orders as to what he should do and where -- mainly, they were digging trenches and so on -- upon which the military police would again take them back from their place of work. Of course, it was dangerous, but it was dangerous in every square centimetre of Busovaca municipality. Remember the testimony of Witness Lukovic who said that it was less dangerous for him to work on the defence line than to be in town, because if you were in town, a shell or grenade would come from somewhere every so often. "Here," he said, "the soldiers took care of us." To illustrate what he said, he added that, in his absence, a shell had entered his flat and hit the room where his grandchildren were. Fortunately, they survived. You see, Your Honours, what can be described as a dangerous spot or a dangerous situation? In the first half of 1993, there was an abundance of dangerous parts. There was hardly a place which was not dangerous. I'm saying this in order to illustrate that interned Muslims from Kaonik did do forced labour under similar conditions as non-interned civilians in the same area, and they did so pursuant to valid regulations of the national legislation. Therefore, it is the contention of the Defence that, as regards forced labour, there was nothing illegal about it per se. It is another matter, however, if those Bosniak Muslims were mistreated while doing forced labour; however, as the Defence has already said, those are events absolutely outside the competence of my client, Mr. Aleksovski. Neither did he order them to be taken to such and such a place, because that was done by the military police, nor did he or his staff have any insight or influence on those locations, nor did those events occur within the Kaonik facility where he was present. Therefore, those are simply facts which I appeal to you to bear in mind when passing judgement on this issue. Human shields. Human shields is another issue that we come across throughout these proceedings. Of course, I'm not going, in any sense of the word, to try and justify the use of people for the purpose of protecting military units with their own bodies. That is something abhorrent, and there is absolutely no justification for such acts. What I am claiming, however, with full responsibility is that there were no human shields. If you analyse the statements of witnesses who spoke about human shields, you will come to the conclusion, I hope, the same conclusion as the Defence. What happened, in fact, was the witnesses who claimed that they had been used as human shields gave descriptions in answer to direct questions by the Defence how this was carried out. I don't wish to tire you with a reinterpretation of individual witness testimonies, but let me remind you of the main points. It is a fact that the witnesses described three cases: The villages of Strane, Skradno, and Merdani. In all three cases, in all three of these villages, there were no units of the BH army. There was no firing from those villages. People were, indeed, rounded up by the HVO and brought to the vicinity of those villages, but they were positioned at a distance 500 to 800 metres from the village on two occasions, and on the third occasion, the village could not be seen from their position because the configuration of the terrain is such that the village cannot be seen. Nobody was injured or killed. One bullet was fired, according to the testimony of one witness, and he doesn't know from where. Now the Defence asks itself the question: Were those really human shields in the sense of the word in which the Prosecutor interprets this phrase? The Defence alleges that they were not. The Defence goes further and wants to say that we accept the possibility that an individual, an irresponsible member of the HVO may have had the idea to use those people as human shields, but it is quite clear that that idea was not consummated, as we lawyers would say, in other words, that no unlawful act occurred and that in this case, we have a classical example of a futile attempt. As I say, they may have had the idea to use them as human shields, but because of the absence of consequences or because of the fact that the attempt was made in relation to an inadequate objective, we cannot consider this as a criminal act but as an attempt that failed. We know that such attempts are not punishable by law. It is the opinion of the Defence that within this legal category, we should view the charge concerning human shields. Finally, allow me to go back to the key issue of this trial. It is the question of an international armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, before going on to the key issue, would you prefer us to have a break? Perhaps that would be a better idea so as not to interrupt the dynamics of your argument. Very well. We shall have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed, and we are listening to you with interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I shall continue my presentation and will thereby be concluding my closing remarks. The opinion of the Defence is that one of the key questions, if not the key question, is the question of the international armed conflict. I said something about this in my introduction, and I am going now to add on to what I said. An international armed conflict, according to the definition in the Geneva Conventions of 1949, expressly demands that an armed conflict take place between two or more countries, high-contracting parties. Article 2 of the Statute of this Tribunal, in keeping with the decision made in the Tadic Appeals Chamber, regulates this question, the question of international armed conflict. The Defence considers that, at the critical time in the area covered by the indictment, there is no question of an international armed conflict. The Defence goes even further than that and claims that not even on the rest of the territory, outside Central Bosnia, that is, in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that at the critical time there was not a state which could be qualified as an international armed conflict. Similarly, the Defence considers that, in the area covered by the indictment, there was not a state of partial occupation either because "partial occupation," by its very definition, represents a situation -- and it is different to an invasion -- when the hostile enemy territory is placed under the control of the attacking army. For us therefore to fulfil the legal and factual conditions indicating the existence of a state of partial occupation, we would have to prove that the attacking army had taken over the entire or part of the territory of the State of the other high-contracting party, according to the definitions of the Geneva Conventions. The Defence firmly considers that an international armed conflict quite simply cannot be applicable to the case in point. By saying this, the Defence indicates the application of rights and law, and the Defence indicates that the relevant law for application in the given case is the law of the Second Hague Protocol and not the Geneva 1949 Conventions. In order to understand the mutual relationships existing between two States, the sovereign State of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a member of the United Nations, on one side, and the Republic of Croatia, also a sovereign State and a member of the United Nations, on the other side, for which it is considered, according to the indictment, that it is a party in the international conflict, we must view what kind of relationships prevailed at the critical point in time, the relationships that prevailed between these two States. Although I am quite certain that the events are well-known to you, allow me nonetheless briefly to remind you of the following: The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed its independence and autonomy from the former State of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the 6th of April, 1992. On the following day, that is to say, the 7th of April, the Republic of Croatia recognised the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina proclaimed in this way. At the end of 1992, on the 28th of November, Charge d'Affaires of the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb was appointed. He was Mr. Kulenovic. At the end of the year, in December, Dr. Sancevic went to Sarajevo to occupy Sarajevo, passing through the well-known tunnel below the airport runway and gave his accreditations to Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the first foreign diplomat to present his credentials. After that, relations between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, without interruption, evolved at the level of embassies. From that point onwards, the point that I mentioned, from that day, which includes the period of hostilities between the Bosniak Croats and the Bosniak Muslims, not at any single point were these diplomatic relations between the two States severed. Even more, these relations were constantly promoted. In January 1993, in Zagreb, Mrs. Bisera Turkovic was accredited as the ambassador in the Republic of Croatia. The presidents of the two States, Tudjman and Izetbegovic, maintained constant contacts, they exchanged many letters, they took part in many meetings. President Izebegovic, in 1993, that is to say, at the time of the most fierce hostilities between the Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats, on several occasions visited the capital of Croatia, had talks there with President Tudjman, had talks with other politicians, and those relations were never severed, not at any point. Quite the contrary. The Croatian parliament, on several occasions, in declarative form, requested that the hostilities be stopped between the Bosniak Muslims and Croats. Efforts were undertaken to stop the hostilities, but events in the area, unfortunately, escaped the political supervision, good wishes, and control. Your Honours, may I remind you of the following: The outbreak of war between two States, which would be in line with an international armed conflict as put forward by the Prosecution, has, as its consequence, the severance of diplomatic and consular relations. Nothing similar occurred in relations between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia. Furthermore, the outbreak of war has an important influence and effect on various agreements existing between States. They are suspended, placed ad acta, but none of this happened. At the critical time, in fact, what happened was that new agreements were signed which included military and peacetime cooperation. May I now remind you of one fact, according to the Defence, an important decision of Article 2 of the Fourth Geneva Convention. This Article is a very important objective test for the existence of a state of war between two States, and it states: "The citizens of a neutral State, finding themselves on the territory of one warring side, country, and the citizens of a State taking part in the war will not be considered as protected individuals until that State whose citizens they are has regular diplomatic representative offices in the State in which they are located." That means, Your Honours, that one warring side would undertake measures towards the citizens of the other State with which it is at war if those citizens are on its territory. May I also remind you that on the 8th of May, 1992, the Republic of Croatia gave shelter to 225.000 displaced persons, refugees, from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Of that figure, which is 5 per cent of the population of the Republic of Croatia, 80 per cent were Muslims. Not a single individual was repatriated nor was any individual's property confiscated, whether it be a physical person or legal person, and all this took place in a situation of a state of war between two sovereign States. If this Trial Chamber were to accept the assertions of the Prosecution that in the given case between the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia that it was a question of a war conflict, then it would be a unique example in history whereby two States were warring against each other whereas, at the same time, they had regular diplomatic relations and, at the same time, took care of the refugees from the State with which they were allegedly at war. Something of that kind has not been known in history and something of that kind did not take place. There was no international armed conflict. That being so, allow me to remind you of some of the evidence put forward by the Defence and which the Defence tendered into evidence in the course of the hearing. First of all, let me remind you of D7, Defence Exhibit D7. It was an agreement on cooperation and friendship between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, and it was dated the 21st of July, 1992. This agreement was signed in Zagreb by Presidents Tudjman and Izetbegovic. On the basis of that agreement, it is stated expressly that the HVO is a component part of the armed forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina and that the provisional civilian authority within the HVO, as soon as possible, would align itself with the constitutional and legal order of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now, why is that stipulated in that particular agreement? It is stipulated because the central authority in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was, in fact, de facto and de jure, incapacitated for action. The central political authority, power and authority, was placed in Sarajevo, Sarajevo was under fierce Serbian occupation, and the central power and authority was not able to function. For that reason, for life to be able to evolve normally in the area outside Sarajevo, various provisional forms of civilian and military administration were developed which are mentioned in the agreement and for which both presidents agreed upon, that as soon as conditions allow, that is to say, as soon as the central government began functioning, be dovetailed with it. Defence Exhibit D9. The date is the 2nd of April, 1993. The time is the time of the conflict between Bosnian Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia. Once again, an agreement, it is between Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Boban by which, after Mr. Izetbegovic had signed the Vance-Owen Plan, established a joint command of the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a part of the military formations, which, in certain regions of Bosnia, were conflicting. Document D8 is an appeal by President Tudjman for hostilities between Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia to cease, and they referred to and hospitality was offered for having a meeting between Izetbegovic, Boban, and Lord Owen in Zagreb as the venue, on the 24th of April, 1993. As I said, throughout this time in Zagreb, the capital of the Republic of Croatia, the Embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina functioned throughout this time. Document D11, Defence Exhibit D11, tendered by the Defence indicates that attached to -- the Embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb was functioning, and I'm speaking about mid 1993. We saw the functioning of a logistics department of the staff of the supreme command of Bosnia-Herzegovina and on the territory of the State for which the Prosecution maintains was a conflicting party in an international armed conflict. This document indicates that such a conflict at the level of two States did not exist. I ask you once again, Your Honours, have you ever heard of a case in history whereby one country warring with another country would have its supreme command staff headquarters in the country that it was allegedly fighting against? That has never existed. Your Honours, let me remind you of a document which the Defence tendered as exhibits in this proceeding, and I'm referring to Exhibits D29 and D30. These are the documents which the Defence received from the Prosecution, and it is an express request to disclose them as exculpatory material. These documents are confidential in nature and, therefore, they are under seal, and the Defence has undertaken an obligation not to disclose them to the public. I would like to remind you of them, but I believe that it is not necessary to move to a closed session, with your agreement, and let me just refer you to these documents without referring to their contents, and I would urge you to study them carefully. However, I wish to point out that these are very relevant documents and which support the theory of the Defence that the relations between the two States were flowing uninterruptedly, even during the conflict between the Croats and Muslims in Central Bosnia, and they were functioning uninterruptedly, both at the level of consulates and embassies and military. Let me refer you to Dr. Bianchini's testimony who said that any aid, military or humanitarian, that entered Bosnia had to go through Croatia, every last piece of weapon, bullet, et cetera. So I ask you what country would have offered this type of assistance if it was in a state of armed conflict? No such case exists in history. Let me point out document D13, which may be one of the most relevant documents. It is dated 21 April, 1993, only five days after Ahmici, that is, at the time of the escalation of conflict in Central Bosnia with a number of casualties and destruction. This document was drafted by Mr. Muhamed Sacirbey, who was the Bosnian ambassador to the U.N. I'm not going to quote the entire document, but let me point out the crucial paragraphs there. In this document, which was sent to the Security Council of the U.N., he describes the Bosnian Croat conflict in Central Bosnia as a conflict of the local leaders due to the shortages of humanitarian aid in the area and insufficient arms, and he says that the cooperation between the BH army and the HVO will continue. Now, this is an official position of the Bosnian government as spelled out by their official representative with the United Nations. This is a document which reflects the position of the official Bosnian government, and if this is not so, I cannot think of a piece of evidence that would stronger support the view that the Defence submits. The Defence would like to point out that in this case, it is not possible to implement Article 2 of the Statute because there was no international conflict in the area at the time covered by the indictment. Finally, let me very briefly refer to the submission of the Defence. The Defence submits that all charges in the indictment should be dropped. Since there was no armed conflict, Article 2 of the Statute does not apply, as well as points 8 and 10. The Defence asks that Mr. Aleksovski be acquitted on all these charges because of the lack of criminal responsibility in the case against Mr. Aleksovski [portion not translated]. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. You don't have to apologise because you haven't offended anyone. This is your task, and we understand it very well. We have therefore come to a point when we have to ask the Prosecutor and the Defence whether they have any intention to present a rebuttal or rejoinder. We're going to work until 6.00, and perhaps we could share this time. I'm not King Solomon, but we could divide up the time between the two parties. I think that that would be a good procedure if you so wish, if you wish to take advantage of the time available, which would mean that we would have perhaps a break midway, not now, but when we get halfway, so we have another hour and a half left. One and a half hours means, for the two parties, 45 minutes for each, but if we deduct from that at least a quarter of an hour, then roughly each side would have 35 minutes. Because when we say "15 minutes," it's usually 20 minutes for the break. So we'll take off ten minutes from the Prosecution, ten minutes from the Defence, and then each will have 35 minutes. Is that acceptable? Do you agree, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As I said yesterday, there will be a number of matters which were raised by Mr. Mikulicic which we would disagree with, but the position that we would take in the Prosecution is that if we've argued it, we don't want to go back and argue it again to Your Honour because our point is that we've made our point, Mr. Mikulicic has made his, we are in disagreement, and we just leave it to Your Honours to resolve. I have a few points which I would say are new. If I take longer than ten minutes, I would be surprised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. We are giving you, in any case, 35 minutes for the Prosecution and 35 minutes for the Defence. It is up to you to manage that time. If you need only ten minutes, then the Defence still has its 35 minutes. Do you agree, Mr. Mikulicic, with this procedure, this manner of resolving this problem? It is a Solomonic solution, but I think it is a good one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I quite agree, even though it is not a Solomonic solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: In that case, Mr. Prosecutor, you have 35 minutes. If you wish to take up only ten minutes' time, it's up to you. Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. Your Honours, I wish to just touch on a few matters which were raised by my learned colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, in his submissions. First of all, he spoke of ethnic hatred and the fact that this could not be attributed to the accused on the basis that he lived in the town of Zenica, which was a town occupied by a large proportion of Muslim people. Well, Your Honours, I just ask you to consider that it's often a strange issue, the question of motive, and it's not always as clear-cut and as easy as that. We've had already one case before this Tribunal of Tadic, where the accused lived in a village of Kozarac which was predominantly Muslim, and nevertheless, he was convicted of the charges that were levelled against him in relation to that. Your Honours, Mr. Mikulicic also suggested to you that with relation to our reliance upon the Celebici and other decisions, that because the appeal process had not run its course, that therefore the decisions were sub judice. We respectfully disagree with that and submit to Your Honours that, of course, you can refer to these cases and of course you can rely on them. We are not for one minute suggesting that they are binding on you, but they are persuasive and certainly reliable, and I just point to the fact that, for example, the accused are presently incarcerated on the basis of those binding orders. So they certainly have effect and they are certainly legally valid, and, indeed, we don't know whether an appeal is going to take place or not. In our submission, the references to Celebici should not in any way be discredited because of the fact that the appeal process has not yet been completed. Your Honours, a reference was made to the fact, and it was, I think, put more or less as an inference by Mr. Mikulicic, that the division between the ethnic communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina somehow or other arose because the International Community endeavoured, at least initially, to resolve the problem based on drawing up a division between the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The only comment I make about that is, the International Community did not operate in a vacuum. It acted upon what it was presented with when it went there in an attempt to resolve the inter-ethnic conflict, and this was merely a reflection, in our submission, of the position of the parties which, at that stage, the International Community thought it may be able to resolve by that course. Any suggestions that the International Community caused the conflict, Your Honours, is, in fact, inaccurate. Mr. Mikulicic made reference to the agreement between Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Izetbegovic in 1992. In our submission, that has little to do with the conflict that subsequently ensued in January and onwards in 1993. We don't for one minute detract from the fact that there was an ongoing relationship between the parties and that, in fact, this agreement occurred in 1992, but this has little to do with the ultimate conflict between the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the HV, and the HVO. Mr. Mikulicic made reference to the lack of corroboration of medical evidence. Your Honours, I covered this in my submission, but I just merely say that both in the Celebici and Tadic cases and the Akayesu case which I referred to, the Trial Chambers in all of those cases came to the conclusion that there was no requirement under international law to have corroboration and that, indeed, it was entirely appropriate to rely upon the testimony of eyewitnesses. Mr. Mikulicic made reference to the Korematsu and Hirabayashi cases in the United States. I just comment on that, Your Honours, that this was a 1942 situation which operated before the 1949 Geneva Conventions. We have moved somewhat further since then, and, Your Honours, I made specific reference in my submissions to the position taken by the Chamber in Celebici which did come to the very firm conclusion that people could not be interned. It was illegal to intern civilians, especially when it's done on the basis of their ethnicity. Your Honours, the question of international armed conflict that was finally touched upon by Mr. Mikulicic when he told us about the exchange of ambassadors, which I think perhaps it's the first time I've heard about that, but in any event, in our submission, that doesn't in any way, so far as I know of the law of this matter, impact upon the question of whether or not there is an international armed conflict. Strange things happen in the world of international diplomacy, and States do sometimes maintain and carry on relationships, notwithstanding the existence of a war operating between them. Whether this is the first time in history, in my submission, is of no consequence at the end of the day in the determination of whether or not an international armed conflict existed. As I said to Your Honours, and I referred to the decision again in the Celebici case, where Their Honours concluded that an international armed conflict could be established if a difference between two States leads to the intervention of the military forces of those States, and it didn't matter how long the conflict continued for or how many people were killed in the process. You may recall I mentioned that to Your Honours. Excuse me, Your Honours. Thank you, Your Honours. Those are the matters I wished to touch upon, unless there is any other matter I can assist you with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, you lived up to our expectations regarding your capacity for synthesis. Mr. Mikulicic, it is your turn now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I shall be even more brief than my learned friend, Mr. Niemann. I think a great deal has already been said and that you now have an overview of the events, but just a few points. When I referred to the fact that Mr. Aleksovski grew up in Zenica, I stressed that this in itself was not a key factor, but it did influence the formation of his personality as somebody who mostly socialised with Bosniak Muslims and whose best friend belonged to that ethnic group. That is only in that context that I mentioned it. Of course, the fact in itself means nothing, but in this particular case, it means what I have just said. Of course, I didn't say that the International Community had provoked the conflict in Bosnia by their behaviour and mediation in the Konak Villa in Sarajevo and later on with the Vance-Owen Plan, I just said that that too was one of the causes of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. History will show what weight that fact had in relation to the conflict. This is something that history will be able to judge from a certain time distance; it is too recent an event for us to be able to fully judge it. But I think you will agree that such an initial approach had some bearing. Of course, the maintenance of diplomatic relations at the embassy level excludes the possibility of an international armed conflict. Why? Because according to the definition in the Geneva Conventions, there is an international armed conflict either when one or other State declares war, and this hasn't happened since 1945, or if at least one of the warring parties become conscious of a state of war. The fact that both parties exchanged ambassadors and maintained diplomatic relations at the level of embassies and consulates, clearly points to the conclusion that neither side was conscious of the existence of an international armed conflict. I think that is a logical conclusion. When I spoke about medical documents which would be objective evidence of injuries sustained by internees in Kaonik, I had in mind, as I think I said, I had in mind the national standards, according to national legislation, and linking this up with the individual liability of the accused civilians, pursuant to national laws regarding criminal offences, and those are those serious criminal offences that I mentioned in my closing arguments. This submission has another side to it, and that is, that in the absence of such documentation on injuries, it is impossible objectively to verify the kind of injuries sustained, how they were sustained, whether they are injuries at all, and of what nature. Therefore, if a person says, "I was seriously injured," that cannot be checked or verified. You will agree that this is a decisive fact which is a decisive element of the criminal offence and which must be subject to objective verification. The truth in this case is not in the eye of the beholder but in the eye of objective and scientific verification. That is all I have to say. I thank you once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So we have come to the end of a part of our work but we haven't really come to the end. In terms of Article 87, the Chamber is going to deliberate in closed session, and we will announce the date when we will deliver our judgement. For the moment, I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to thank the parties for their ardour, their conviction, their motivation, and the cooperation with which you approached the debate. I also thank all the personnel, the technical booth, the interpreters, the court reporters, and the registry personnel for all their cooperation. As for the Judges, our duty now is to draft our judgement and, as I have said, we will announce the date. For the moment, in accordance with Article 87, I declare closed the debate, and we are going to withdraw to deliberate. Therefore, thank you all, until our next meeting here for passing down judgement. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 4.47 p.m. sine die
